caseno: Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No. 1138 of 2006.
lawyer:
Md Nawab Ali, Advocate-on-Record--For the Petitioners. 
Not represented---The Respondents.
parties:
Kulsuma Khatun ------ Petitioner
vs
Rahman Sobhan ------ Respondent
case_source: (From the judgment and order dated 5-7-2006 passed by the High Court Division in Civil Revision No. 4334 of 1998).
full_judgment:
Md Joynul Abedin J: This petition for leave to appeal is directed against the judgment and order dated 5-7-2006 passed by a Single Bench of the High Court Division in Civil Revision No. 4334 of 1998 discharging the Rule.

2. The short fact leading to the filing of the leave petition is that the suit land is originally recorded as Government khas land during the time of CS operation. The suit land was sold in auction for arrear of rent in Certificate Case No. 25/20-21 on 11-9-1922 and auction-purchased by one Abala Sundari in the benami of Upendra Lal Chowdhury and Prafulla Bala Debi and got delivery of possession through Court. Upendra Lal Chowdhury by registered deed dated 22-9-1922 relinquished his claim in favour of Abala Sundari and Abala Sundari got delivery of possession on 31-5-1923. Prafulla Bala by registered kabala dated 22-9-1930 sold her share of land to Abala Sundari and delivered possession to her. RS Khatian finally stands recorded in the name of Abala Sundari. The suit land was hillock and full of jungle. Abala Sundari converted the same by expending huge amount of money. Abala Sundari while in possession made an agreement for sale with the predecessor of the plaintiffs with a consideration money of Taka 2500 and she took Taka 2000 as advance and delivered possession to plaintiffs' predecessor on 26th of Kartik, 1340 BS. After purchase the predecessor of the plaintiffs constructed kutcha and pucca houses upon the schedule land and he was in peaceful possession. After the death of their predecessor the plaintiffs are in possession upon the suit schedule land and they acquired title over the same under section 54 (A) of the Transfer of Property Act. The defendant Nos. 2 to 14 have got no right, title, interest and possession over the suit land but they have fraudulently managed to have their names recorded in the BS khatian and now they are claiming title over the suit land. Hence the plaintiffs filed the present suit for declaration of their title.

3. The defendant did not appear in the suit in spite of due notice and, as such, the learned trial Court took up the suit for ex parte hearing and by Order No. 1 dated 23-3-1991 the trial Court decreed the suit ex parte. Against this ex parte decree, Rahman Sobban and Farooque Sobhan filed Miscellaneous Case No. 32 of 1991 under Order IX, rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure.

4. The learned Assistant Judge by order No. 46 dated 15-10-1992 dismissed the said Miscellaneous case. As against this order, the defendant Nos. 1 and 2 filed Miscellaneous Appeal No. 310 of 1992 and by judgment and decree dated 23-8-1998, the learned Subordinate Judge, 3rd Court, Chittagong allowed the appeal on setting aside the judgment and order dated 15-10-1992 and restored Title Suit No. 183 of 1990 to its original file and number. Thereafter the plaintiff-petitioners, filed a review petition before the same Court to reconsider and set aside the judgment and order passed on 23-8-1998, which was ultimately rejected on 22-11-1998. Thereafter the plaintiff-petitioners having been aggrieved by the judgment and order dated 23-11-1998 preferred Civil Revision No. 4334 of 1998 in the High Court Division. After hearing the learned Single Judge of the High Court Division discharged the Rule. Thereafter being aggrieved and dissatisfied with the impugned judgment and order of the High Court Division the plaintiff-petitioners filed this civil petition for leave to appeal.

<u>5. Mr Md Nawab Ali, the learned Advocate-on-Record for the petitioners, submits that the case of the defendant-respondent Nos. 1 and 2 before the trial Court was that the summons was not duly served on them and that they were not aware of the institution of the suit but they did not claim in their petition that their addresses given in the cause-title of the suit was wrong but in spite of this position the learned Subordinate Judge as well as the learned Single Judge of the High Court Division committed an error of law resulting in an error in the decision occasioning failure of justice in making out a third case. He lastly, submits that the Single Bench of the High Court Division committed an error of law affirming the judgment and order of the appellate Court below without any legal and valid reasonings. Therefore the judgment of the High Court Division is liable to be set aside for the ends of justice.</u>

6. We have heard the learned Advocate and perused the connected papers including the impugned judgment. We do not find any substance in the points raised. The High Court Division upon correct assessment of the materials on record arrived at a correct decision. We therefore find no reason to interfere with the same.

The petition is accordingly, dismissed.

End.

lawyer:
Garib Nawaz, Advocate—For the Petitioner. 
Habibul Islam Bhuiyan, with Md Faruque Ahmed, Advocates — For the Opposite Party No. 1.
parties:
Delwar Hossain Khan ------ Petitioner
vs
Amzad Hossain and others ------ Opposite Parties
full_judgment:
Badrul Huq J: The short but substantial question that survives for determination in this Rule arising out of an application under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure is, whether the court below was well founded in law within the ambit of section 9 of the Specific Relief Act in awarding a decree of recovery of possession with respect to the suit property in favour of the plaintiff-opposite-party.

2. The question involved and the decision proposed to be given does not call for a detailed re-counting of facts except that the defendant-petitioner laid a suit being Title Suit No. 59 of 1992 in the Second Court of Subordinate Judge, Dhaka for a decree of specific performance of contract with respect to the property described in the schedule to the plaint of the suit in our hand impleading Dasu Roy Chowdhury and others as defendants. The said suit was decreed on compromise on 14-9-1992. In pursuance of the compromise decree execution case being Title Execution Case No. 29 of 1993 had been started by the decree-holder-defendant-petitioners who took delivery of possession on the suit property through process of the court.

3. The plaintiff-opposite parties who were not parties in the previous Title Suit No. 59 of 1992 instituted the present suit being Title Suit No. 102 of 1995 under section 9 of the Specific Relief Act in the Second Court of Subordinate Judge, Dhaka for recovery of khas possession on the said suit property. The suit was, thereafter, transferred to the court of additional sub-ordinate Judge, Dhaka and re-numbered there as Title Suit No. 9 of 1996. The learned additional sub-ordinate Judge, Dhaka decreed the suit in favour of the plaintiff-opposite-parties and directed the present defendant-petitioners to hand over the possession of the suit property in favour of the plaintiff-opposite-parties.

4. Feeling aggrieved of the above adjudication, the defendant-petitioners approached this Court in an application under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure and obtained the present Rule.

5. Mr Garib Newaz, the learned Advocate appeared in support of the Rule. The plaintiff-opposite parties are represented by Mr Habibul Islam Bhuiyan assisted by Mr Md Faruque Ahmed, the learned Advocate.

6. The sustainability of the judgment and decree recorded by the learned Trial Judge was assailed from the side of the defendant-petitioners raising the contention that the plaintiff-opposite parties having been dispossessed by the court in due process of law, the suit laid by the plaintiff-opposite parties was not at all maintainable and the learned trial Judge committed a substantial error in awarding a decree in favour of the plaintiff-opposite parties directing the defendant-petitioners to hand over the possession of the suit property in favour of the former.

7. The only submission pressed into service from the side of the plaintiff-opposite-parties is that the suit so framed under section 9 of the Specific Relief Act can be converted into a Miscellaneous Case under rule 100 of Order 21 of the Code of Civil Procedure in the exercise of this Court''s power under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure.

8. We first of all propose to address ourselves to the contention raised from the side of the defendant-petitioner. To appreciate this contention it will be profitable to look at the Provision of Section 9 of the Specific Relief Act which is quoted here under:

"9. Suit By Person Dispossessed of Immoveable Property: If any person is dispossessed without his consent of immovable property otherwise than in due course of law, he or any person claiming through him may, by suit recover possession thereof, notwithstanding any other title that may be set up in such suit.

Nothing in this section shall bar any person from suing to establish his title to such property and to recover possession thereof.

No suit under this section shall be brought against the Government.

No appeal shall lie from any order or decree passed in any suit instituted under this section, nor shall any review of any such order or decree be allowed."

9. From a plain reading of the said Provision it becomes manifestly clear that if a person who has without his consent, been dispossessed of immovable property otherwise than in due course of law, he is entitled to recover possession thereof by filing a suit within the period of 6(six) months of dispossession.

<u>10. Section 9 of the Act has been enacted to prevent persons from evicting men from possession except through due process of law. It is a section the object of which is to drive a person who wants to dispossess person and prevent him from going with a high hand and dispossessing such person. This section is more than a re-production of the provisions of Roman Law by which the Praetor was entitled to restore possession to a person forcibly dispossessed. The question, therefore, in a case under section 9 of the Specific Relief Act is, whether a person while in physical possession of an immovable property has been dispossessed of the same otherwise than in due course of law and if so dispossessed he can be restored to such possession under the decree of the court if the suit is instituted within the period stipulated in the section which is 6(six) months.</u>

<u>11. The expression "due course of law" means the regular, normal process and effect of the law operating on a matter which has been laid before a court for adjudication. That is the regular, normal course and operation of the law invoked by the method of a civil Court through judicial proceeding. In this context, it is to be borne in mind that the expression "due course of law" is not synonymous with the word ''legal''.</u>

<u>12. Keeping in view the above principle it is now to be seen whether the plaintiff-opposite parties were dispossessed from the suit property otherwise than in due course of law. From the pleadings, evidences and materials brought on record it appears that in pursuance of a Title Execution Case No. 29 of 1993 arising out of a decree for Specific Performance of Contract in Title Suit No. 56 of 1992, the defendant-petitioners were inducted into possession through process of the court which is definitely in due process of law. To put it differently, the plaintiff opposite parties had been dispossessed with the intervention of the court and the said dispossession cannot be at all characterized as otherwise than in due course of law. Since the plaintiff-opposite parties had been dispossessed and defendant-petitioner was inducted into possession on the suit property through the process of law, the dispossession is not otherwise than in due course of law and a suit under section 9 of the Specific Relief Act was not at all maintainable.</u>

13. On perusal of the judgment under challenge it is seen that the learned trial Judge failed to notice the scope of section 9 of the Specific Relief Act and travelled beyond his jurisdiction in deciding a suit under section 9 of the Specific Relief Act over-looking and ignoring the scope of the said section. The learned trial Judge unnecessarily took into consideration matters which were absolutely beyond the ambit in deciding a suit of summary nature like the present one. The manner in which the trial Judge disposed of the suit is very much disapproved by us. The contention advanced from the side of the defendant-petitioner is accepted.

<u>14. Coming now to the contention raised from the side of the plaintiff-opposite-parties that the suit framed under section 9 of the Specific Relief Act can be converted into a Miscellaneous Case under the provision of rule 100 of Order 21 of the Code of Civil Procedure cannot be accepted inasmuch as this Court exercising power under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure got no scope to convert a suit under section 9 of the Specific Relief Act into a Miscellaneous Case under rule 100 of Order 21 of the Code of Civil Procedure.</u>

<u>15. Rules 100 and 101 of Order 21 of the Code may conveniently be seen which are extracted below.</u>

<u>Rule 100 of Order 21:</u>

<u>"100.-(1) Where any person other than the judgment-debtor is dispossessed of immovable property by the holder of a decree for the possession of such property or, where such property has been sold in execution of a decree, by the purchaser thereof, he may make an application to the Court complaining of such dispossession.</u>

<u>(2) The Court shall fix a day for investigating the matter and shall summon the party against whom the application is made to appear and answer the same."</u>

<u>Rule 101 of Order 21:</u>

<u>"101. Where the Court is satisfied that the applicant was in possession of the property on his own account or on account of some person other than the judgment-debtor, it shall direct that the applicant be put into possession of the property."</u>

<u>16. From the language of the two Rules it becomes evidently clear that when an application under Order 21, rule 100 is made the court shall register the application, make an investigation therein and the court, if satisfied that the applicant was in possession of the property of his own account or on account of some persons other than the judgment debtor it shall direct the applicant be put into possession of the property. The court in the Rule is the executing court and the right to apply arises only after the applicant has been dispossessed and the application is to be presented before the court within thirty (30) days from the date of dispossession as mandated in Article 165 of Schedule 1 of The Limitation Act, 1980.</u>

<u>17. From the materials on record it appeared that the writ of delivery of possession was executed on 5-11-1994 and the decree holders-defendants-petitioners were inducted into possession on the Suit Property on 5-11-1994. Law enjoins the laying of an application under Rule 100 within 30 days of the date of dispossession. But no such application had been filed before the court within the said stipulated time. Suit under section 9 of the Specific Relief Act has been laid on 20-4-1995. Judgment and decree recorded in the said suit was on 18-1-1999. The suit framed under section 9 of the Specific Relief Act is a Title Suit, though, summary in nature. But an application under Order 21, rule 100 of the Code takes the form of a Miscellaneous Proceedings. Even before the court below there is no scope of converting the suit under section 9 of the Specific Relief Act into a Miscellaneous Proceeding under Order 21, rule 100 of the Code. So the question of converting the suit under section 9 of the Specific Relief Act into a Miscellaneous Proceeding under Order 21, rule 100 of the Code does not at all arise. In this context it is to be remembered that no litigant has a right to get his affairs settled in the manner as he wishes. Every access to justice must not be used as a licence to a litigant. The contention so raised from the side of the plaintiff-opposite-parties, thus, stands rejected.</u>

18. The impugned judgment recorded by the court below appears to have suffered from serious legal infirmity and a flagrant error of law as the scope and ambit of section 9 of the Specific Relief Act was misunderstood rendering the same unsustainable.

19. Resultantly, the conclusion that flows is that the Rule got merit and the same, thus, succeeds. The Rule is, accordingly, made absolute. The impugned judgment and decree recorded by the learned trial Judge is set aside and the suit stands dismissed.

20. No costs.

LCR be sent down immediately.

End.

Vs.

case_source: (From the judgment and order dated 20-6-2005 passed by the High Court Division in Civil Revision No. 2384 of 1991).
full_judgment:
MM Ruhul Amin J: This petition for leave to appeal is directed against the judgment and order dated 20-6-2005 passed by a Single Bench of the High Court Division in Civil Revision No. 2384 of 1991 making the Rule absolute.

2. Short facts are, that father of the petitioners filed Title Suit No. 58 of 1970 in the 6th Court of Munsif (now Assistant Judge), Barisal. The suit was decreed ex parte on 16-1-1971. The respondent No.1 brought Miscellaneous Case No. 15 of 1990 under Order IX, rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure for setting aside the ex-parte decree on the ground that the summonses of original suit was not duly served upon the defendants and the names and addresses of the defendants were wrong and the summonses were shown served in collusion with the process server. The petitioners resisted the said application by filing written objection denying the material averments of the application and stating, inter alia, that the summons of the original suit was duly served and the ex parte decree was rightly passed since the defendants failed to appear and contest the suit. They further contended that the miscellaneous case was barred by limitation having been brought after 19 years of the ex-parte decree by the son of one of the original defendants after his death. Their further case is that one Abdul Kader, the defendant No. 3 in the said original Title Suit, brought a similar case against the same ex-parte decree being Miscellaneous Case No. 7 of 1971 which was dismissed on 24-3-1972. Thereafter, the second case brought by the son of another defendant (since deceased) is barred by principle of res judicata and hence the same is not maintainable.

3. The trial court allowed the Miscellaneous Case No. 15 of 1990 under Order IX, rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure. Being aggrieved the respondent moved the High Court Division and the High Court Division after hearing made the Rule absolute.

4. We have heard Mr. Md. Nawab Ali, the learned Advocate-on-Record for the petitioner and perused the judgment of the High Court Division and other connected papers.

<u>5. The High Court Division held that an application under Order 9 Rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure for setting aside the ex parte decree is to be brought within 30 days from the date of ex-parte decree or from the date of knowledge of the aggrieved party. In the instant case, the Miscellaneous Case No.15 of 1990 was brought long after 21 years of the ex-parte decree. The High Court Division further held that the father and husband of the present petitioner did not bring any such case against the ex-parte decree. The case was brought after 21 years of the ex parte decree stating that they came to know of the ex-parte decree on 15th Falgoon, 1396 BS. The High Court Division in this connection considered the evidence of PW 1, PW 2 and PW 3 in the Miscellaneous Case and held that they failed to prove that the petitioner knew about ex parte decree on 15th Falgoon, 1396 BS. The High Court Division also observed that earlier the respondent's cousin brought Miscellaneous Case No. 7 of 1971 for setting aside the same ex-parte decree but the same was dismissed on 24-3-1972.</u>

<u>6. Considering the above facts and circumstances of the case, the High Court Division found that the Miscellaneous Case was barred by both limitation as well as by principle of res judicata and accordingly, made the Rule absolute.</u>

<u>7. We have considered the materials on record and the submissions of the learned Advocate-on-Record. In the facts and circumstances of the case, we are of the view that the High Court Division upon correct assessment of the materials on record arrived at a correct decision, that miscellaneous case was barred by limitation. There is no cogent reason to interfere with the same.</u>

<u>Accordingly, the leave petition is dismissed.</u>

End.

lawyer:
Md Muzammel Hossain, with Md Raziuddin Sarwar, Advocates—For the Petitioner. 
Md Raziur Rahman Chowdhury with Muhammad Abdul Majid, Advocates — For the Opposite Party Nos. 1-8.
parties:
Chairman, Bangladesh Agricultural Development Corporation ------ Petitioner
Vs
Abedunnessa & others ------ Opposite Parties
full_judgment:
Feeling aggrieved by a decision of the First Court of Assistant Judge, Dhaka in a suit for declaration of Title and recovery of Khas possession, refusing to reject the plaint under the provision of Order VII, rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure, the defendant-petitioner approached this Court in an application under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure whereupon a Rule was issued calling upon the Opposite party Nos. 1-8 to show cause as to why the order dated 20-3-1994 passed by the First Court of Assistant Judge, Dhaka in Title Suit No. 290 of 1984 should not be set aside.

2. The only question that falls for determination in this Rule is whether the impugned decision in refusing to reject the plaint under the provision of Order VII, rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure warrants any interference in the exercise of Revisional jurisdiction under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure.

3. For the purpose of answering the said question posed, the factual canvass of the matter may be adverted to. The opposite party Nos. 1-8 as plaintiffs instituted a suit being Title Suit No. 290 of 1984 in the First Court of Munsif (now Assistant Judge), Dhaka for a declaration that the plaintiffs are entitled to get the suit land as described in schedule to the plaint on derequisition of the same in their favour. The defendant-petitioner has been impleaded as defendant No. 3. The Government of the People's Republic of Bangladesh represented by the Secretary, Ministry of Works, Bangladesh Sachibalaya, Dhaka has been impleaded as defendant No.1 The plaintiffs in the plaint stated, inter alia, that in the year 1958-59, the suit property along with other properties owned and possessed by them was requisitioned by the Government in LA Case No. 30 of 1958-59. The suit land was not utilised for the purpose for which it was requisitioned and, as such, they are entitled to get back their land. The plaintiffs made several representations to the Government for derequisitioning the said land but they failed in getting the land derequisitioned.

4. The defendant-petitioner entered appearance in the suit by filing power but did not ultimately contest the suit by filing written statement. The suit was, thereafter, decreed ex parte in favour of plaintiff-opposite-parties.

5. The defendant-petitioner, against the said decree, carried an appeal being Title Appeal No.7 of 1985 in the Court of District Judge, Dhaka with an application for condonation of delay. The learned Additional District Judge, Third Court, Dhaka heard the appeal, dismissed the same and maintained the ex parte decree passed by the learned Assistant Judge.

6. The defendant-petitioner, thereafter, moved a Revisional application being numbered as Civil Revision No. 29 of 1987 before the High Court Division and obtained Rule. In the said Civil Revision High Court Division recorded the following findings:

(a) The defendant has been sued for its act of taking lease of the suit property and this act is no doubt an act purported to be done under the Corporation and a notice in writing must be given before bringing any suit against BADC as per section 74 of the Ordinance.

(b) It could not be said that a prima facie case for decree for derequisitioning the suitland has not been made out.

(c) From the conduct of the plaintiffs it could not be said that the plaintiffs tried to commit any fraud. With the above findings the High Court Division set aside both the judgments and decrees of the Courts below and remanded the suit to the trial court for hearing the same in accordance with law. The Rule was, accordingly, made absolute.

7. The record of the suit having been received by the trial Court, the defendant-petitioner filed an application for rejection of the plaint under Order VII, rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure taking the ground that requirement of law for mandatory notice upon the defendant-petitioner as mandated under section 74 of BADC of Ordinance, 1961 had not been followed and the plaint is liable to be rejected as being barred by law. The next ground taken is that, the BADC is a juristic person but instead of the Corporation, the Chairman of the said Corporation had been made a defendant and the plaintiffs having no cause of action against the Chairman, the plaint is liable to be rejected. The last ground taken is that the suit for declaration simpliciter is hit by the proviso to section 42 of the Specific Relief Act and there being no cause of action, the plaint is liable to be rejected.

8. The plaintiff-opposite-parties contested the said application by filing written objection stating that the defendant No.3 appeared in the trial Court from the very beginning and contested the suit although before the appellate Court and the Hon'ble High Court Division but nowhere the defendant ever raised any such objection giving right to the rejection of plaint. It is also averred that the notice to the defendant No.3, although was not felt necessary at the time of institution of the suit, was subsequently sent to it after the order of Hon'ble High Court Division in Civil Revision Case No. 29 of 1987. It is also pleaded that in order to restore the property back from the defendant No.1 the plaintiffs instituted the aforesaid suit for release of their properties.

9. The learned Assistant Judge held that had the suit been barred by law, the Hon'ble High Court Division would not have sent the suit back on remand for retrial and decision. The learned Assistant Judge further held that the suit having been sent on remand to the trial Court, notice under section 74 of the said Ordinance had been issued upon the defendant and so the defect, if any, stood cured. The learned Assistant Judge also recorded the finding that the Chairman of the Corporation has been made a defendant only and it is not stated that Corporation is represented by its Chairman and from the record it is manifested that the Corporation has been contesting the suit and any omision in the plaint can be corrected and amended and for that reason the plaint cannot be rejected. With the above decisions, the learned Assistant Judge refused to reject the plaint and rejected the application of the defendant-petitioner filed under Order VII, rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure.

10. The defendant-petitioner challenged the propriety of the said decision of the learned Assistant Judge in an application under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure and obtained the present Rule.

11. The plaintiff-opposite-parties resisted the Rule by filing an affidavit-in-opposition. In the affidavit-in-opposition it is stated that the plaintiffs filed the suit challenging the acquisition vis-a-vis the leasing out of the property for a purpose other than the purpose for which it was acquisitioned and also prayed for khas possession. It is also stated that the plaintiff-opposite-parties in accordance with the provisions of the said Ordinance, 1961 served notice upon the BADC in compliance with the order of the Hon'ble High Court Division by a legal notice dated 2-12-1993. It is also asserted that the suit is not barred under the provision of the said Ordinance of 1961 nor under section 42 of the Specific Relief Act.

12. The defendant-petitioner is represented by the learned Advocate Mr Md Mozammel Hossain. The plaintiff-opposite-party Nos. 1-8 are represented by the learned Advocate Mr Md Raziur Rahman Chowdhury.

13. Since the question of the rejection of the plaint under the provisions of Order VII, rule 11 of the Code is involved in this Rule, the said provision may profitably be noticed first before adverting to the contentions advanced from both the sides.

14. Order VII, rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure reads thus:

" 1. The plaint shall be rejected in the following cases:

(a)	Where it does not disclose a cause of action:

(b) Where the relief claimed is undervalued, and the plaintiff, on being required by the Court to correct the valuation within a time to be fixed by the Court fails to do so:

(c) Where the relief claimed is properly valued, but the plaint is written upon paper insufficiently stamped, and the plaintiff, on being required by the Court to supply the requisite stamp-paper within a time to be fixed by the Court, fails to do so:

(d) Where the suit appears from the statement in the plaint to be barred by any law: Provided that the time fixed by the Court for the correction of the valuation or supplying of the requisite stamp paper shall exceed twenty-one days."

15. Rule 11(a) enjoins that a plaint can be rejected where it does not disclose a cause of action. Rule 11(b) provides that a plaint can be rejected where the relief claimed is under-valued and the plaintiff on being required by the court to correct the valuation within a time to be fixed by the Court fails to do so. Rule 11(c) manifests that a plaint can be rejected where the relief claimed is properly valued but the plaint is written upon paper insufficiently stamped and the plaintiff on being required by the court to supply the requisite stamp paper within a time to be fixed by the court fails to do so. Rule 11(d) authorizes the rejection of the plaint where the suit appears from the statements in the plaint to be barred by any law. This provision applies when it appears from the statements in the plaint that the suit is barred but it has no application where there is no clear or specific admission in the plaint suggesting that the suit is barred.

16. The first branch of contention advanced on behalf of the defendant-petitioner is that the mandatory provision of notice as required under section 74 of Ordinance of 1961 having not been served upon the defendant-petitioner before the institution of the suit, the suit is barred by law and the same is liable to be rejected and the learned Assistant Judge committed an error in not rejecting the plaint. In support of the said contention reliance has been placed upon Bangladesh Agricultural Development Corporation vs Md Mannaf Hossain Khan and others, 36 DLR (AD) 69.

17. In repelling the said contention raised, the learned Advocate for the plaintiff-opposite-parties, on the other hand, submitted that no act purporting to be done under the said Ordinance having not been challenged by the plaintiffs in the suit, they are not at all required to issue any notice under section 74 of the Ordinance before the institution of the suit. The plaintiffs only prayed for declaration that the plaintiffs are entitled to get the suit lands derequisitioned in their favour and also for a recovery of khas possession against defendants and the relief has been mainly directed against the defendant No.1, the Government of the People''s Republic of Bangladesh who requisitioned the suit property, the learned Advocate further submitted.

18. In reply to the said contention raised from the side of the plaintiff-opposite-parties, it is canvassed from the side of the defendant-petitioner that under sub-section 2 of section 3 of the Ordinance the Corporation being a body corporate got the power subject to the provisions of the Ordinance to acquire and hold property both movable and immovable and the suit land having been leased out by the Government in favour of the defendant petitioner the latter acquired and held the property and the acquisition and holding of the property is an act purporting to be done under the Ordinance and, as such, the plaintiffs cannot escape from serving notice under section 74 of the Ordinance.

19. In the wake of rival contentions raised from both the sides it is profitable to quote section 74 and section 3(2) of the Ordinance of 1961. Section 74 of the said Ordinance runs thus:

"74. Notice of suit against the Corporation, etc (1)

No suit shall be instituted against the Corporation, the Chairman, any Director, any person associated with the Corporation or any officer, adviser or servant of the Corporation, or any person acting under the direction of the Corporation, of the Chairman or of any officer or servant of the Corporation in respect of an act purporting to be done under this Ordinance, until after the expiration of two months next from notice in writing has been, in the case of the Corporation left at its office, and in any other case delivered to or left at the office or place of abode of the person to be sued, explicitly stating the cause of action, the nature of the relief sought, the amount of compensation claimed, and the name and place of abode of the intending plaintiff; and in case the suit is filed, the plaint shall contain a statement that such notice has been so delivered or left.

(2) If the Corporation or other person referred to in sub-section (1) shall before the action is commenced, have tendered, in the opinion of the Court, sufficient amends to the plaintiff, the plaintiff shall not recover any sum in excess of the amount so tendered and shall also pay all costs incurred by the defendant after such tender.

(3) Action such as is described in sub-section (1) shall, unless it is in action for the recovery of immovable property or for a declaration of the title there to be commenced within six months next after the accrual of the cause of action. Provided that nothing in this section shall be construed to apply to suit wherein the only relief claimed is an injunction of which the object would be defeated by the giving of the notice or the postponement of the commencement of the suit or proceedings."

20. Section 3(2) of the said Ordinance runs thus:

"3(2). The Corporation shall be a body corporate having perpetual succession and a common seal, with power, subject to the provisions of this Ordinance, to acquire and hold property both movable and immovable, and shall by the said name sue and be sued."

21. From a plain reading of the provisions of section 74 it reveals that no suit shall be instituted against the Corporation, the Chairman, any Director, any person associated with the Corporation or any officer, adviser or servant of the Corporation, or any person acting under the direction of the Corporation, of the Chairman or of any officer or servant of the Corporation in respect of an act purporting to be done under this Ordinance, until after the expiration of two months next from notice in writing has been, in the case of the Corporation left at its office, and in any other case delivered to or left at the office or place or place of abode of the person to be sued, explicitly stating the cause of action, the nature of the relief sought, the amount of compensation claimed, and the name and place of abode of the intending plaintiff. So, the act must be an act purported to be done by the Corporation under this Ordinance. Sub-section 2 of section 3 of the Ordinance enjoins that subject to the provisions of the Ordinance the Corporation got the power to acquire and hold property both movable and immovable. The word "acquired" means acquisition of property and the word "hold property" means holding of the said property acquired under an acquisition proceeding.

22. Chapter VII of the Ordinance deals with acquisition, abandonment of acquisition and levy of development fee. The said Chapter also deals with the mode of acquisition of property under the Land Acquisition Act, 1894. It is pointed out here that the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 stood repealed with the coming into force of the Acquisition and Requisition of Immovable Property Ordinance, 1982.

23. Keeping in view the provisions detailed above let me now consider whether the institution of the suit by the plaintiffs seeking relief for declaration that the plaintiffs are entitled to get the land derequisitioned in their favour and a decree for recovery of khas possession against the defendant are hit by section 74 of the Ordinance and whether issuance of mandatory notice of two months prior to the institution of suit is a requirement of law.

24. Under sub-section 2 of section 3 of the Ordinance the acquisition and holding of property by the Corporation is attempted to be characterized as an act of the Corporation on behalf of the defendant-petitioner. In the instant case before me the plaintiffs do not challenge any acquisition proceeding and holding of the land by the Corporation. The plaintiffs are seeking declaration of their entitlement for derequisitioning the suit land and admittedly the Government, the defendant No. 1, being the acquiring authority acquired the suit land along with other lands for the sole purpose of a Ring Road to protect the nuclear houses from water in LA Case No. 30 of 1958-59.

<u>25. In the case of Bangladesh Agricultural Development Corporation vs Md Mannaf Hossain Khan and others, 36 DLR (AD) 69 an emplayee of BADC was dismissed from service and the said employee filed a Title suit in the First Court of Subordinate Judge, Dhaka for a declaration that his order of dimissal from service was illegal, void and inoperative and therefore not binding upon him and that he had been still in service. In the said suit no notice contemplated under section 74 by the said Ordinance was served by the plaintiff upon the Corporation. The plaintiff in the suit challenged the order of dismissal and, as such, the direct act of the Corporation had been called in question. In the said case it is held that sub-section 3 of section 74 of the Ordinance does not contemplate suit for recovery of possession of Immovable property and for declaration of title thereto as held by the learned Judges of the High Court Division and obviously their interpretation of section 74 is misconcieved. In the case in my hand no act of the Corporation has been challenged in the suit by the plaintiffs. The plaintiffs prayed for declaration that they are entitled to get the suit lands derequisitioned in their favour and also for a decree of khas possession. The said case is of no assistance to the defendant-petitioner. It is significant to remember that every judgment must be read as applicable to the particular fact assumed and the generality of the expression used must be read as qualified by the particular fact of the case.</u>

<u>26. Having given my anxious consideration to the fact, circumstances and also keeping in view the relevant provision of law, I am of this considered view that since no act of the Corporation has been challenged by the plaintiffs in the suit, they were not required to serve any notice as contemplated under section 74 of the Ordinance of 1961 and the plaint also cannot be rejected for non-service of notice under the said section of the said Ordinance. The first branch of contention advanced on behalf of the defendant-petitioner, thus, fails.</u>

27. Coming now to the second branch of contention advanced from the side of the defendant-petitioner that Bangladesh Agricultural Development Corporation is a juristic person and under sub-section 2 of section 3, the Corporation may sue and be sued and since the plaintiffs instead of making the Corporation defendant made the Chairman of the said Corporation defendant, the suit is not maintainable and the plaint is liable to be rejected as being barred by law. The learned Advocate has referred to an unreported case in Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No. 26 of 1992, Md Arphan Ali being petitioner and Sonali Bank and others being respondents, in support of the contention raised.

28. In reply it is submitted on behalf of the plaintiff opposite parties that the Chairman is the Chief Executive of the Corporation and as the Chairman of the Corporation he preferred the appeal as well as the Civil Revision before the High Court Division and also filed the application for rejection of the plaint and impleading the Chairman of the Corporation in place of the Corporation itself is a mere technicality and by this technicality a plaint cannot be rejected. In support of the contention reliance has been placed on M Rashiduzzaman vs Government of Bangladesh and others, 49 DLR 43.

29. In view of the contention raised, the question now comes whether the plaint can be rejected under Order VII, rule 11 of the Code for impleading the Chairman of the Corporation instead of the Corporation itself. In sub-section 2 of section 3 of the Ordinance it is coined that the Corporation shall be a body corporate having perpetual succession and a common seal with power subject to the provision of this Ordinance to acquire and hold property both movable and immovable and shall by the said name sue and be sued. In this context it will be appropriate to notice section 72 of the Ordinance which is as under:

72. Power of the Chairman as to institution, etc. of legal proceedings and obtaining legal advice. The Chairman may, subject to the control of the Corporation.

(i) Institute, defend or withdraw from legal proceedings under this Ordinance;

(ii) Compound any offence against this Ordinance;

(iii) Admit, compromise or withdraw any claim made under this Ordinance; and

(vi) obtain such legal advice and assistance as he may, from time to time deem it necessary or expedient to obtain, or as may desired by the Corporation to obtain, for any of the purposes referred to in the foregoing claims of this section, or for securing the lawful exercise or discharge of any power or duty vested in or imposed upon the Corporation or any officer or servant of the Corporation."

30. Section 72(i) enjoins that the Chairman may subject to the control of the Corporation institute, defend or withdraw from legal proceedings under this Ordinance. From the said provision it is manifestly clear that the Chairman as the highest functionary of the Corporation can institute and defend any legal proceeding under this Ordinance.

<u>31. In Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No. 26 of 1992 as referred to from the side of the defendant-petitioner, the Chief Cashier of the Elephant Road Branch of Sonali Bank on a charge of misappropriation of money was dismissed from service. The Chief Cashier filed Administrative Tribunal Case before the Administrative Tribunal, Dhaka only impleading Assistant General Manager, Sonali Bank as defendant No.1 but did not implead Sonali Bank, his employer as a party to the petition. Thereafter, by way of an amendment, in place of Assistant General Manager, Sonali Bank was substituted. The Appellate Tribunal who allowed the amendment found at the time of hearing that the case was time barred because Sonali Bank was substituted after one year and four months of the impugned order and dismissed the appeal. Their Lordships of the Appellate Division held that Sonali Bank is a legal entity whereas its Assistant General Manager is not and if the petitioner''s case was allowed, the Assistant General Manager had no authority to reinstate him. In the instant case the plaintiffs impleaded the Chairman who is the Chief functionary of the Corporation whereas in referred Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal, Assistant General Manager was not the chief functionary.</u>

The fact and circumstances of the Civil petition is quite distinguishable and got no manner of application in the fact and circumstances of the present case. In the case of M Rashiduzzaman vs Government of Bangladesh and others, 49 DLR 43 as referred to from the side of the plaintiff-opposite parties, the prayer of the petitioner, an employee of Bangladesh Biman Corporation, for voluntary retirement was refused and he ventilated his grievance before the High Court Division in Writ petition under Article 102 of the Constitution making the Managing Director of Bangladesh Biman and other persons as respondents but did not implead Bangladesh Biman Corporation as respondents. In the Writ petition plea was raised from the side of the respondents that since Bangladesh Biman Corporation is a body corporate which can sue and be sued and has not been made a party, the writ petition is not maintainable. The High Court Division held that the Managing Director is in fact, representing the Bangladesh Biman Corporation and the objection being a very technical objection, will not frustrate the purpose of the writ petition. In the present suit the Chairman is representing the Corporation as the Chief functionary and, as such, the objection that instead of the Corporation itself, the Chairman is made defendant in the suit is a technical objection. It is posited here that the contention raised is a question of maintainability which does not come within the four walls of the provisions of Order VII, rule 11 of the Code and this question of maintainability can be agitated by the defendant-petitioner at the time of hearing of the suit. The second branch of contention is, also, devoid of any substance.

32. Turning now to the third and the last branch of contention that the trial Court granted the decree of recovery of khas possession without realising the advalorem court fee and only court fee of Taka 30.00 had been paid. Submission has been pressed into service from the side of the plaintiff-opposite parties that in view of the direction made by the lower appellate Court, the requisite court fee of Taka 1464.00 had been deposited in the court on 18-11-1986. In support of the submission the certified copy of the order dated 18-11-1986 showing payment of the said court fee has been placed before me. From the certified copy of the order it appears that court fee of Taka 1464.00 has been paid by the plaintiff-opposite parties. The last branch of contention, also fails.

33. The learned Assistant Judge considered various aspects, facts and circumstances of the case in refusing to reject the plaint under Order VII, rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure and the decisions arrived at by the learned Assistant Judge do not indicate any error of law to have been committed by which a failure of justice has been occasioned.

34. Before parting with the case I am inclined to observe that for the exercise of power under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure as it stands now after Ordinance No. XLVIII of 1983, two conditions are to be satisfied, (i) there must be an error of law resulting in an error in the decision, and, (ii) by that error of law a failure of justice has been occasioned. it is, thus, evidently clear that unless the above two conditions are satisfied no interference is called for by the High Court Division in exercise of the power under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure. Mere error of law is not the only ground for the exercise of the said power and along with the error of law it is to be manifested that a failure of justice has been occasioned. Neither any error of law appears to have committed by the learned Assistant Judge nor any failure of justice has been occasioned by the order under challenge in this Rule. No interference is, therefore, called for.

35. In view of the discussion made herein above I am of this considered view that this Rule is without any merit and the same, thus, fails.

36. In the result, the Rule is discharged.

37. Having regard to the facts and circumstances of the case there will be no order as to cost.

Order of stay stands vacated.

End.

full_judgment:
AK Badrul Huq J: This appeal by the Defendant Nos. 6-9 has been presented challenging the propriety of the judgment and decree dated February 28, 1991 passed by the Second Court of the Subordinate Judge, Chittagong by which the learned Judge awarded decree in favour of the plaintiff in a suit for declaration of exclusive right, title and interest in the suit properties mentioned in Schedule-1 and for further declaration that the suit properties under the provisions of law does not come within the purview of Vested and Non-Resident Properties and also for a decree that the defendant Nos. 1-5 be evicted from the Schedule 1(A), 1(B), 1(C), 1(D) properties respectively and the same be given to the plaintiffs khas possession.

2. The facts relevant for the purpose of deciding the appeal are as follows: Khirod Chandra was the owner of the schedule properties described in the plaint and RS Record of Right stood in his name. Khirod Chandra, thereafter, transferred the suit property in favour of one Aziz Uddin on receipt of full consideration money of Taka 99.00 and put him into possession of the same under a Deed of agreement dated 6-6-1948. In the Deed of agreement stipulation was that within a period of 5 years from the date of execution in the event of repayment of consideration money, the transferee Azizuddin would be bound to recovery the suit property to him and in the event of failure, the said transferee Azizuddin would have acquired absolute right, title, interest therein. Khirod Chandra did not repay the consideration money and also did not have reconveyonce of the suit property within the stipulated period of 5 years and on the expiry of the said period Azizuddin acquired absolute right, title, interest in the property and in assertion of his paramount title had been exercising acts of ownership and possession over the suit property on payment of Government Revenue for more than the statutory period of limitation denying the right, title and interest of all other persons. During the Petty Settlement Operation the Record of Right i.e. PS Khatian has been prepared in the name of Aziz Uddin and he thus acquired a good title over the suit property by adverse possession on being duly recognized as a tenant by the Government. Aziz Uddin, thereafter, being the absolute owner and possessor of the suit property transferred the same in favour of Nur Ahmed and 3 others by a deed of conveyance duly registered on 24-10-1964. Possession was handed over by Aziz Uddin to the said transferees Nur Ahmed and others. The transferee Nur Ahmed and others got their names mutated in the relevant Record of Right in Mutation Case No. 16(1)/69-70. Nur Ahmed, and others being the owners and possessors of the suit property, transferred the same in favour of Joinab Khatun for valuable consideration by way of a sale deed registered on 3-9-1969 and the possession of the suit property was also handed over to Joinab Khatun. Joinab Khatun got her name mutated in the relevant Record of Right in Mutation Case No. 275(T)/76-77. She also got her name recorded in the Municipal Holding. She regularly paid Government rents, Municipal taxes payable in respect of the suit property. Joinab Khatun obtained an approved plan from the Chittagong Development Authority for construction of a two-storied building, made some improvements of the structures standing on the suit property but could not complete the construction as per approved plan. Joinab Khatun also got an electric connection in the house standing on the suit property and the water and electric meters stood in her name. Joinab Khatun while in peaceful and uninterrupted possession for about 30 years including the period of her predecessor vendors out of the schedule property No. 1 let out schedule 1(a) property to the defendant No. 1 as purely temporary monthly tenants under a Deed of agreement of tenancy on 1-9-1972 and the same was renewed on 16-1-1973. The defendant No. 1 occupied the premises on payment of rent to the landlord Joinab Khatun. The defendant No. 1 having defaulted in payment of rent became a defaulter and Joinab Khatun for a bonafide requirement of the said premises terminated the tenancy of the defendant No. 1 and laid Other Suit No. 130 of 1971 in the Court of Second Munsif, Sadar, Chittagong. The defendant No. 1, thereafter, started depositing rents before the House Rent Controller, Chittagong in House Rent Case No. 180/66/95/74. The suit for ejectment was dismissed. Appeal preferred against that also stood dismissed. In the said suit and also the House Rent Control Case, the defendant No.1 admitted Joinab Khatun as his landlord and he also characterised himself as a tenant under landlord Joinab Khatun. The defendant No. 1 with a malafide motive applied to the defendant No. 6, Additional Deputy Commissioner (Revenue), and Custodian, Vested and Non-resident Property, Chittagong stating that Joinab Khatun was his fake landlord and the suit property was vested and Non-Resident Property and he prayed for lease of the said premises. The defendant No. 6 on the basis of the said application started a VP Miscellaneous Case No. 6 of 1977-78.

3. The further case of the plaintiff is that Joinab Khatun being in possession of the suit properties let out part of the schedule-1 property which is described schedule-1(b) to the defendant No. 2 on purely temporary monthly rental basis under a deed of agreement and defendant No. 2 possessed the said tenanted premises purely as a temporary monthly tenant under landlord Joinab Khatun. Defendant No. 3 by way of an application addressed to the defendant No. 6 prayed for granting lease of the suit property with the averment that the property is a Non-Resident and Vested Property. The defendant No. 6 was pleased to make an enquiry into the matter. The vested property Tahsilder conducted an inquiry into the matter and submitted a report to the effect that Joinab Khatun had been exercising acts of possession on the suit property in assertion of her right and the same was not Vested and Non-Resident Property and the same was not included in the list of Non-Resident and Vested Property. The defendant No. 6 on the basis of the Report and also on a note submitted by the Superintendent of the Vested and Non-Resident Property found that the suit property was not included in the Census List. Joinab Khatun, thus, being the absolute owner and possessor of the suit properties transferred the same to the plaintiff by way of 8 sale deeds dated 12-5-79, 14-5-79, 15-5-79, 16-5-79, 19-5-79, 21-5-79, 23-5-79 and 25-5-1979 and placed the plaintiff into exclusive possession of the schedule property, out of the schedule-1 property schedule-1(a) and 1(b) property through temporary monthly tenants defendant No. 1 and 2 respectively and physical possession was given to the plaintiff with respect to the remaining portion i.e., schedule-1(c) and 1(d). The plaintiff on the basis of his purchase got her name mutated in the connected Record of Right in Mutation Case No. 123(1) of 1978-79. Her name has been also mutated in the record of the Municipality and present Municipal Holding stands in her name.

The predecessor vendors of the plaintiff and the plaintiff regularly paid rent to the Government, taxes to Municipal and other taxes to the concerned authorities required by law to pay. The plaintiff has been exercising acts of ownership and possession on the suit property in assertion of her right and title for more than statutory period of limitation to the knowledge of all concerned including the defendants. The defendant No. 2, after the plaintiff''s purchase, entered into a fresh agreement of tenancy with the plaintiff on May 15, 1980 and regularly paid rent to the plaintiff upto the month of August 1980. The defendant No. 1 with malafide motive did not pay rent to the plaintiff and denied to pay the same in-spite of repeated demands made by the plaintiff. The plaintiff, thus, was compelled to determine the tenancy of the defendant No. 1 and filed Other Suit No. 84 of 1980 in the Second Court of Munsif, Chittagong for ejectment of the defendant No. 1 from the schedule-1(a) suit premises. The plaintiff also let out schedule-1(c) property premises to defendant No. 3 purely as temporary monthly tenant under a deed of tenancy agreement dated 15-5-1980 who paid rent to the plaintiff upto the month of July 1980. The defendant No. 3, thereafter, under the evil influence of defendant No. 1 stopped payment of rent to the plaintiff and sub-let to the defendant No. 4 who is no other than the full brother of the defendant No. 3 without the knowledge and consent of the plaintiff. The defendant No. 4 is absolutely a trespasser on the suit premises having no right to continue illegal occupation there. The schedule-1(d) remains still in the possession of the plaintiff and during his temporary absence from the country permitted one Mohammad Ali, a close neighbour to stay on the schedule-1(d) property and to manage and look after the entire schedule-1 property. The defendant No. 5 is a Police Constable and had been in close touch with the said Mohammad Ali who brought him into the schedule-1 (d) premises and permitted to stay therein. Later on he left the said premises leaving defendant No. 5 therein without the knowledge and consent of the plaintiff. The defendant Nos.1-5 now having denied the plaintiff as the lawful owner of the suit property are making attempts to have the suit property declared as Vested and Non-Resident Property. The suit property cannot come under the mischief of Vested Property.

4. Defendant Nos. 6-9 contested the suit by presenting a written statement and stated, inter alia, that the suit is not maintainable in the present form. There is no cause of action for the suit. The suit is barred under sections 42, 54 and 56 of the Specific Relief Act. The suit is also barred by Displaced Persons Compensation and Rehabilitation Act and other laws in force. The stand taken by the defendants are that, Khitish Ghose left for India for good from erstwhile East Pakistan on or before 6-9-1965 and consequently the property became Enemy Property and vested in the custodian as per the provision of Defence of Pakistan Rules. The defendant Nos. 6-9 initiated Vested Property Case No. 6/77-78 to recover possession of the suit property and leased out the same to the deserving persons and, accordingly, the persons in unauthorized possession of the suit property were asked to surrender their possession to the defendants. The suit property was leased out to these defendants. It is pleaded that the plaintiff and his alleged vendors did not acquire any right, title and interest on the suit property.

5. The defendant No. 1 did not file any separate written statement but adopted the written statement filed by the defendant Nos. 6-9.

6. On the basis of the pleadings the following issues had been framed:

1. Is the suit maintainable in its present form?

2. Is the suit barred by res judicata?

3. Is the suit properly valued and duly stamped?

4. Is the suit bad for defect of parties?

5. Is the plaintiff entitled to get a decree as prayed for?

6. What other reliefs, if any, is the plaintiff entitled to?

7. Both the parties led evidence both documentary and oral in support of their respective pleas/contentions. A good number of documents had been exhibited from the side of the plaintiff which are Exhibits-1-19-19. Documents had been also exhibited from the side of defendant Nos. 1 and 6-9 which are Exhibits ''Ka'' to ''Cha''.

8. The witnesses have been examined from the side of the plaintiff. One witness had been examined from the side of the defendant Nos. 6-9 who is DW 1. The defendant No. 1 examined himself as DW 2.

9. PW 1 Md Shahjahan is the son of the plaintiff. He gave testimony in support of the plaintiff''s case on the basis of an authority i.e., the Power of Attorney executed and registered by plaintiff in his favour empowering him to give testimony and to do all things necessary for conducting the suit. The said Power of Attorney is Exhibit-1. He started the plaint case, proved the documents which are exhibited as Exhibits 1-19 series. He also proved the agreement of Tenancy executed by the plaintiff side in favour of the Tenant defendants.

10. PW 2 Mokhter Ahmed is a Moharar of the Office of the District Registrar, Chittagong. He proved the Sale deed dated 24-10-1964 executed by Azizuddin in favour of Nur Ahmed and others and the said deed had been exhibited as Exhibit-16(H).

11. DW 1 is Akbar Khan who was the Chief Tahsilder of the Tahsil Office, Sadar, Chittagong and before that he was Principal Assistant of Chittagong Sadar Vested and Non-Resident Property Department. He gave testimony on behalf of the defendant Nos. 6-9. He testified that on local enquiry the defendant Nos. 1-5 were found in possession of the suit property and notices were issued upon them from the Vested Property Office to hand over possession of the suit property in favour of the Vested Property authority. He proved 4 notices which were exhibited as Exhibit Kha-Kha (3). He also proved some documents which were exhibited as Exhibit Ga, Gha and Uma. In cross-examination he stated that his evidence is mainly on the basis of the record and from the record he stated that Khirod Chandra Ghosh left for India and he got no personal knowledge of the departure of Khirod Chandra Ghosh for India.

12. DW 2 Anwar Mia is defendant No. 1. He stated that he remained in possession of the suit property on the basis of lease from the Government. He denied the ownership of the plaintiff with respect to the suit property and asserted that the suit property is vested property and the Government of Bangladesh is the owner. In cross-examination this witness stated that before taking lease he remained in possession of the suit property and being in possession of the same, he applied for lease to the Government.

13. The learned trial Judge decided all the issues in favour of the plaintiff. Taking into consideration of all the legal evidences, the pleadings and the laws emanating from the facts proved, learned trial Judge recorded the finding that the plaintiff produced the connecting title deeds leading to his acquisition of title over the suit property and filed Rent Receipts and also the Municipal Tax Receipts, Electricity Bill Receipts. On a discussion and assessment of the legal evidence he categorically found that the plaintiff from the time of his vendor predecessors had been in possession of the suit property for more than 40 years and acquired title 17 years prior to coming into force of the Defence of Pakistan Ordinance dated 6-9-1965 and the Rules framed thereunder and as such, they acquired good title by adverse possession also. Further finding is that Nur Ahmed and others acquired title over the suit property before Enemy Property Laws came into force and right, title and interest of Khirod Chandra Ghosh stood extinguished. The learned trial Judge also recorded the finding that the defendants failed to produce Census List evidencing enlistment of the suit property as vested property and also signally failed to prove by legal evidence that Khirod Chandra Ghosh on 6-9-1965 or before that left erstwhile East Pakistan for India and that he had been there as an Indian citizen. With the above findings, the learned trial Judge awarded decree in favour of the plaintiffs.

14. Feeling aggrieved by the decision arrived at by the learned trial Judge, the defendant Nos. 6-9 presented this appeal before this Court.

15. Mr Shahidul Alam Chowdhury, learned Advocate along with the learned Advocate Mr Md Kafiluddin Ahmed appeared in support of the appeal. Respondent-plaintiff is represented by the learned Advocate Mr Shafique Ahmed along with the learned Advocate Mr Saifur Reza.

16. The question that survives for determination in this appeal is, whether the awarding of decree in favour of the plaintiff is well-founded both on law and fact and whether the same warrants any interference by this Court in the exercise of its appellate jurisdiction.

17. Let us now address ourselves to the determination of the question posed. Admittedly, the suit property belonged to Khirod Chandra Ghosh and the RS Record of Right stood in his name. The said Khirod Chandra Ghosh is alleged to have executed an agreement to sale deed dated 6-6-1948. The said agreement to sale deed is exhibit-9. On a plain reading of the Exhibit-9 it transpires that there was a clear stipulation that within a period of 5 years from the date of execution of the said agreement if the consideration money could be repaid to Aziz Uddin, the latter would be bound to recovery/transfer the suit property to the said Khirod Chandra Ghosh and in default Aziz Uddin would acquire absolute right, title and interest therein. It appears that Khirod Chandra Ghosh did not have any reconveyonce of the suit property on payment of consideration money. It manifests that the suit property stood recorded in the name of Aziz Uddin in the subsequent Record of Right i.e., the Petty Settlement Khatian. The Petty Settlement Khatian No. 245 had been prepared in the name of Aziz Uddin. This PS Khatian may not be a document of title but definitely is an evidence of possession at least during the time of preparation of PS Khatian. Exhibit 16(H) is the deed of conveyance executed and registered by Aziz Uddin in favour of Nur Ahmed and others dated 22-10-1964. Exhibit 16(a) is the sale deed dated 13-5-1969 executed by Nur Ahmed and others in favour of Joinab Khatun. Exhibit 16-16(a) are the sale deeds of different dates of the year 1979 executed and registered by Joinab Khatun in favour of the plaintiff. PS Khatian is exhibit-10. Exhibit-3 is the corrected Record of Right prepared in the name of Nur Ahmed and others in Mutation Case No. 16(1) of 1969-70. From the said exhibit-3 it transpires that the name of Joinab Khatun had been also mutated with respect to the suit property Khatian in Mutation Case No. 275(T)/76-77. Exhibit-17 is the record evidencing that the plaintiff''s name had been mutated in the connected Record of Right in Mutation Case No. 123(1) of 1978-79. Exhibit-5 is the assessment list evidencing assessment by Municipal Authority with respect to the suit property in the name of Joinab Khatun. Exhibit 6 series are Rent Receipts evidencing the payment of rent to the Government since the year 1960. On the face of these massive evidences as to the acquisition of title by the plaintiff side over the suit property it cannot be at all suggested that the plaintiff side did not and could not acquire any right, title and interest over the suit property merely because the agreement deed dated 6-6-1948 is not a registered instrument. The plaintiff could connect his acquisition of title starting from 1948 to 1979. The learned trial Judge considered all the legal evidences and appears to have come to a correct decision in holding that the plaintiff side acquired good title over the suit property at least by way of acquisition of title by adverse possession as they remained in possession for more than 40 years since the year 1948. No exception can be taken to the said decision.

<u>18. Let us now direct our attention to the next question whether the defendant Nos. 1-5 remained in possession on the basis of a lease granted to them by the Vested Property authority i.e. the defendant Nos. 6-9. Exhibit 12 is the certified copy of the judgment passed in Other Appeal No. 265 of 1977 arising out of Other Suit No. 180 of 1976. This appeal was directed against the judgment and decree passed in Other Suit No. 180 of 1976 which was filed by Joinab Khatun against the defendant No. 1 for eviction. It transpires from the said judgment that the suit and the appeal arising out of the suit stood dismissed. But the fact remains that the defendant No. 1 in the said suit in his written statement admitted Joinab Khatun as his landlord and he also described himself as a tenant under Joinab Khatun. Now it does not lie in the mouth of the defendant No. 1 that Joinab Khatun and the transferee, the plaintiff is not the owner of the suit property and the Government is the owner of the same. The conduct of the defendant No. 1 appears to be absolutely malafide. Being inducted as a tenant he attempted to turn down this title of his landlord setting up a claim that the suit premises where he stayed as a tenant under Joinab Khatun is owned by the Government as Vested Property. Exhibit-8 is an agreement of tenancy entered into between the plaintiff and defendant No. 2. Exhibit-8(A) is the agreement of tenancy in between the plaintiff and the defendant No. 3. In both the Exhibits 8 and 8(A) the defendant Nos. 2 and 3 admitted the plaintiff as the landlord owner of the suit property. It is unfortunate that these defendants also attempted to have lease of their suit premises treating it as Vested Property. The defendant No. 4 is alleged to have been inducted into a portion of the suit property by his brother, the defendant No. 3 who was a tenant under the plaintiff and the defendant No. 5 was also inducted in the suit property unauthorized behind the back of the plaintiff. The learned trial Judge appears to have recorded the correct finding that the defendant No. 5 is a trespasser on the suit property.</u>

19. Now comes the last question whether the suit property can at all come under the mischief of Enemy Property and whether the said property can be treated as Vested Property. It has been already pointed out that the predecessor vendors of the plaintiff and, thereafter, the plaintiff exercised acts of ownership and possession over the suit property for more than a period of 40 years till the institution of the suit in the year 1981. It has been also pointed out that some defendants are tenants under the plaintiff and some are trespassers. On a perusal of order-sheets exhibit 15 it appears that the Vested Property authority did not enlist the suit property as Vested Property in the Census List. No legal evidence came forth from the side of the defendants that the original owner Khirod Chandra Ghosh left this country on 6-9-1965 or prior to that date. The loss of domicile of origin by Khirod Chandra Ghosh and his acquisition of Indian citizenship could not be at all substantiated and proved by any legal evidence. DW 1 as witness for the defendant Nos. 6-9 categorically stated that he got no personal knowledge of the departure of Khirod Chandra Ghosh from this country on 6-9-1965 or prior to that. The foundation of treating the suit property as Vested Property thus fell to the ground.

<u>20. On 6-9-1965 Emergency was proclaimed by the then President of the then Pakistan who declared that grave emergency existed and Pakistan was in eminent danger of being threatened by war. Further declaration was that Pakistan was at War with India. In pursuance of the Declaration of Emergency the then President of Pakistan promulgated Defence of Pakistan Ordinance, 1965. Rules were framed thereunder called the Defence of Pakistan Rules. The Emergency and the Defence of Pakistan Ordinance and the Rules framed thereunder continued till 16th of February 1969 when came the formal declaration of the revocation of the Proclamation of Emergency and the Proclamation of Emergency dated 6th September, 1965 ceased to exist and Ordinance No. 1 of 1969 came into force thereafter. There cannot be any question of supposed continuation of said war after 16th February 1969. If any action, therefore, is sought to be taken with regard to any property after 16th February, 1969 as Enemy Property (Vested Property) it is to be seen whether the property sought to be taken over as Enemy Property (Vested Property) was so between 6-9-1965 to 16-2-1969 and there cannot be any vesting of property as Enemy Property (Vested Property) after 16-2-1969. No paper had been produced from the side of the defendants evidencing that the suit property was enlisted in the Census List as Enemy Property (Vested Property). Treating a property as Enemy Property on the basis of an Enemy Property Case started in the year 1977 is not valid at all. The learned trial Judge duly considered this legal aspect of the matter and arrived at correct decision with respect to the treating of the suit property as vested property.</u>

21. Before parting with the judgment we are inclined to observe that now a days specially in urban and city areas there is a tendency on the part of persons who had been inducted into possession of a premises/ house/building in any way to litigate and consume time as an umbrella for continuation of illegal possession on the premises. The present case before us is a glaring example how the defendant Nos. 1-5 specially the defendant No.1 admitting the plaintiff as owner of the suit property, in a malafide way engineered and hatched up a conspiracy to cement their illegal occupation on the suit property in taking lease on treating the property as Vested Property. This type of tendency on the part of the defendants must be discarded and also penalised. The trial Judge did not award any cost against the defendant No. 1. This Court as the appellate Court got all the powers of a trial Court and, as such, we award a cost of Taka 5,000.00 against the defendant No. 1 to be paid to the plaintiff.

22. What emerges from the above discussion is that the appeal got no merit and the same must fail.

23. The appeal is, accordingly, dismissed with cost.

LC Records be sent down at once.

End.
