full_judgment:
Sheikh Abdul Awal J: By this Rule the opposite Party No. 1 was called upon to show cause as to why the impugned order dated 16-7-2008 passed by the learned Joint District Judge, 1st Court, Dhaka in Title Execution Case No. 14 of 2006 rejecting the application filed by the petitioners under Order XXI rule 26 of the Code of Civil Procedure for staying all further proceedings of Title Execution Case No. 14 of 2006 should not be set-aside.

2. Relevant facts, in short, are that the present petitioners as plaintiffs instituted Title Suit No. 370 of 2007 in the Court of learned Joint District Judge, 1st Court, Dhaka against the opposite parties imp leading them as defendants praying a decree to the effect that the plaintiffs are the sixteen annas owner of the kaga schedule property as described in the schedule of the plaint and also for setting aside the ex parte decree dated 12-1-2004 passed in Title Suit No. 85 of 1999.

3. The opposite party No. 1 as plaintiff after obtaining ex parte decree dated 12-1-2004 passed in Title Suit No. 85 of 1999 put the decree into execution by filing Title Execution Case No. 14 of 2006 before the learned Joint District Judge, 1st Court, Dhaka.

4. During the pendency of the said execution case the present petitioners 3rd party filed an application under Order XXI rule 26 of the Code of Civil Procedure for staying all further proceeding of the Code of Civil Procedure for staying all further proceeding of the execution Case till disposal of the Title Suit No. 370 of 2007.

5. The executing Court upon hearing the parties and on considering the materials on record rejected the said application by its order dated 16-7-2008.

6. Being aggrieved by the aforesaid order dated 16-7-2008 the present petitioners have come before this Court and obtained the present Rule.

7. Mr Kabirul Islam Fakir, the learned Advocate appearing for the petitioners submits that the executing Court without considering the facts and circumstances of the case under misconception of law most illegally rejected the application filed by the present petitioners under Order XXI rule 26 CPC. He next in the course of argument after placing the provisional application and other materials on record including the impugned order dated 16-7-2008 submits that the present petitioners as plaintiffs filed Title Suit No. 370 of 2007 for setting-aside the ex parte judgment and decree of Title Suit No. 85 of 1999 and during pendency of the said Title Suit if the execution Case is completed by executing and registering the sale deed and handing over formal possession through Court the Title Suit No. 370 of 2007 would be frustrated and its result would be ineffective but the executing Court without considering the aspect of the case mechanically rejected the application for staying all further proceedings of Title Execution Case No. 14 of 2006 which resulted in the failure of justice and, as such, the impugned order is liable to be set-aside.

8. Mr Kabirul Islam Fakir, the learned Advocate finally submits that the executing Court ought to have considered that the petitioners are the owner and possessors of the suit properties and they filed Title Suit No. 370 of 2007 challenging the ex parte judgment and decree of Title Suit No. 85 of 1999, if the execution case arising out of ex parte judgment and decree of Title Suit No. 85 of 1999 is not stayed till disposal of the Title Suit No. 370 of 2007 the whole purpose of the Title Suit No. 370 of 2007 would be frustrated.

9. On the other hand, Mr Abdul Quddus Miah, the learned Advocate appearing for the decree-holder, opposite party No. 1 relying on the decisions reported in 49 DLR 526 and 56 DLR (AD) 139 supports the impugned order which was, according to him just, correct and proper.

10. We have heard the learned Advocates, perused the Provisional application, counter affidavit and other connected papers as filed therewith. As already noticed that during the pendency of the execution case the present petitioners as 3rd party filed an application for staying all further proceedings of Title Execution Case No. 14 of 2006 arising out of Title Suit No. 85 of 1999 stating, inter alia, that on knowing about the said ex parte dectiee the petitioners as plaintiffs filed Title Suit No. 370 of 2007 before the learned Joint District Judge, 1st Court, Dhaka for setting aside the said ex parte decree and in such situation if the proceedings of the execution case is not stayed the whole purpose of Title Suit No. 370 of 2007 would be frustrated.

11. The learned Joint District Judge, 1st Court, Dhaka on considering the application and the provisions of Order XXI rule 26 and 29 CPC rejected the application by his Order No. 17 dated 26-7-2008 stating as follows:

দেঃকাঃবিঃ আইনের ২১ আদেশের ২৬ ও ২৯ নিয়মের বিধান অনুযায়ী শুধুমাত্র Judgment-debtor কোন মামলা দায়ের করিলে সেইক্ষেত্রে আদালত আইনগত ব্যবস্থা গ্রহণ করিতে পারে তবে কোন অবস্থাতেই তৃতীয়পক্ষ দেঃকাঃবিঃ আইনের ২১ আদেশের ২৬ ও ২৯ নিয়ম অনুযায়ী মামলা দায়ের করিয়া জারী মামলার কার্যাক্রম stay চাইতে পারে না। বিধায় দরখাস্তকারীগণ কর্তৃক আনীত অত্র জারী মামলার কার্যক্রম stay সংক্রান্ত দরখাস্ত না-মঞ্জুর করা হইল।

12. Now, the real question for consideration in this Case is, whether the executing Court acted wrongly in holding that the petitioners being a third party to the decree has no locus standi to maintain an application for stay of the execution proceeding as per provisions of order XXI rule 26 and 29 of the Code of Civil Procedure.

13. In deciding this question, we feel it necessary to quote hereunder the provisions of Order XXI rule 26 and 29 CPC.

14. Order XXI rule 26 CPC reads as follows:

(1) The Court to which a decree has been sent for execution shall, upon sufficient cause being shown, stay the execution of such decree for a reasonable time, to enable the judgment-debtor to apply to the Court by which the decree was passed, or to any Court having appellate jurisdiction in respect of the decree or the execution thereof, for an order to stay execution, or for any other order relating to the decree or execution which might have been made by such Court of first instance or appellate Court if execution had been issued thereby, or if application for execution had been made thereto.

(2) Where the property or person of the judgment-debtor has been seized under an execution the Court which issued the execution may order the restitution of such property or the discharge of such person pending the result of the application.

(3) before making an order to stay execution or for the restitution of property or the discharge of the judgment-debtor, the Court may require such security from, or impose such conditions upon, the judgment-debtor as it thinks fit.

15. Order XXI rule 29 CPC reads as follows:

"Where a suit is pending in any Court against the holder of a decree of such Court, on the part of the person against whom the decree was passed, the Court may, on such terms as to security for otherwise, as it things fit, stay execution of the decree until the pending suit has been decided."

16. From a plane reading of the aforesaid provisions, it manifests that an application for staying the execution of a decree till disposal of the pending suit is only attracted which the subsequent suit is pending before the same Court who passed the decree in the previous suit and it must be filed by the judgment debtor.

<u>17. In the instant case the petitioners being a third party of the ex parte decree filed an application under Order XXI rule 26 and 29 of the Code of Civil Procedure for staying all further proceedings of execution Case till disposal of the Title Suit No. 370 of 2007 and therefore, we are of the opinion that the executing Court in the facts and circumstances of the case rightly arrived at a finding that petitioners being a third party to the decree have no locus standi to file an application under Order XXI rule 26 and 29 of the Code of Civil Procedure for staying all further proceedings of Execution Case till disposal of the title Suit No. 370 of 2007. We endorse the reasoning given by the executing Court in rejecting the application under Order XXI rule 26 and 29 of the Code of Civil Procedure for stay.</u>

18. Mr Kabirul Islam, the learned Advocate appearing for the petitioner failed to point out any illegality in the findings of the executing Court which may call for our interference, the impugned order is based on proper appreciation of law and fact.

19. In the result, the Rule is discharged without any order as to cost. The order of stay granted earlier by this Court stands vacated the executing Court is directed to proceed with the execution case expeditiously.

Communicate this judgment at once.

End.

Nabibur Rahman Choudhury being dead his heirs-Sayeda Khatun & ors ------ Respondents
full_judgment:
This appeal under section 100 of the Code of Civil Procedure is directed against the judgment and decree passed by Subordinate Judge, Second Additional Court, Sylhet reversing the decision of the learned Munsif, Additional Court, Sylhet in a suit for declaration for title and recovery of khas possession on the suit land.

2. The defendant No. 1 is the appellant and the plaintiffs are respondents.

3. Put briefly, the case of the plaintiffs is that the suit land measuring 0.25 acres of land appertaining to Taluk No. 6299/20 Lal Mohammad belonged to their father Khalilur Rahman Chowdhury. The suit land was marshy and grass growing for grazing cattle. During Cadestral Survey Operation, the suit land was recorded in plot No. 2943 in the name of their father, Khalilur Rahman as son and Jebunessa as daughter. Muktabisur Rahman, thereafter, died leaving behind defendant Nos. 2-4. Jebunessa died leaving behind defendant No.5. The suit land fell in the share of the plaintiffs by amicable arrangement amongst the heirs of Khalilur Rahman and they exercised acts of possession on the suit land by growing paddy. During the Survey Settlement Operation, the defendant No.1 collusively got his name recorded in respect of the said 0.35 acres of land. The plaintiffs, thereupon, filed an objection case and the same was dismissed. Plaintiffs, thereafter, filed an appeal under section 19(2) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act and the same was allowed on 31-5-1966 with the order that the land be recorded in the name of the plaintiffs. Against the said decision, the defendant No. 1 preferred a special appeal which was decided against the plaintiffs. On 31st day of May, 1966 the defendant No. 1 having attempted to dispossess the plaintiffs, the latter filed a case against the defendant No. 1 under section 144 of the Code of Criminal Procedure and the said case was later on converted into a case under section 145 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. In the said 145 proceeding the possession of the suit was found with the plaintiffs. The plaintiff''s criminal case against the defendant No. 1 under section 379 of the Penal Code which was filed for reaping away paddy from the suit land by the defendants was dismissed. The defendant No. 1 being encouraged with the order dated 31-5-1996 passed in the special appeal forcibly dismissed the plaintiff in the middle part of the month of Poush, 1373 BS which compelled the plaintiffs to file the suit.

4. The defendant No. 1 contested the suit by presenting a written statement traversing all the allegations made in the plaint. In the written statement it is stated that the suit land appertained to Taluk No.702/29 Patta Md Afsar originally belonged to Obaidur Rahman Choudhury in Maliki right and the suit land had been recorded in Cadestral Survey plot No. 2941. It is specifically pleaded that Obaidul Rahman Chowdhury was in khas possession of the plot No.2943 and he settled the said plot No. 2943 to the defendant No. 1 35 years back at a rent of Taka 6 and the defendant has been possessing the same openly and adversely by growing paddy therein. It is also averred that he paid rent to the superior landlords and received Farogs (Rend receipts) from the landlords. It is further stated that the adjacent eastern plot of CS Dag No.2943 is CS Dag No.2828 which appertained to Taluk No.6299 Lal Mohammad and the said plot was purchased by the father of the plaintiffs. It is the further case of the defendant that during the Survey Settlement Operation the entire land of CS Dag No.2943 was recorded as settlement survey Dag No.389 in the name of the defendant No.1. The plea of limitation and adverse possession have been also taken by the defendant No. 1 in the written statement.

5. Over the said pleadings the parties fought out the suit.

6. In support of the respective claim contention both the parties filed documentary evidences and also led oral evidences Three witnesses have been examined from the side of the plaintiffs including the plaintiff No. 1 himself as PW 1. The defendant No. 1 only examined himself as DW 1. No other witnesses have been examined to substantiate the claim of the defendant No.1.

7. The learned trial judge held that the contesting defendant could not file any document in support of his contention as to title and ownership on the land of CS Dag No. 2943. The learned trial judge then recorded the finding that CS Dag No. 2943 was originally jungle kind of land which led him to believe that while the defendant No.1 had been possessing the CS Dag No. 2943 he cleared the jungle and amalgamated the suit land with his own land and the plaintiffs having found the suit land as good Boro land, they became alert and filed so many cases to get the land under their possession from the possession of the defendant but they could nowhere succeed. The learned trial judge was of the view that since it is not denied that the defendant has been possessing contiguous western land of the suit land for a long time, about 35 years, he was constrained to hold that he has been possessing the suit land for the last 35 years as contended by him. The learned trial judge was, also, of the view that the documentary evidence of possession of the defendant in the suit land has also shown that the defendant has been possessing the suit land since long time. The learned trial Judge ultimately came to the finding that the plaintiff''s title to the suit land became barred since the defendant has been in possession thereof adversely against the statutory period of limitation and the suit stands barred by limitation and the prayer of the plaintiffs for recovery of khas possession of the suit land is also not tenable. With the above finding and views the learned trial Judge dismissed the suit.

8. The plaintiffs carried an appeal against the said decision of the learned trial Judge to the Court of District Judge, Sylhet. The learned Subordinate Judge, Additional Second Court, Sylhet heard the appeal and concurred with the decision of the learned trial Judge on the question of title and held that the learned Munsif had rightly opined that the defendant No. 1 failed to prove title in the suit land by any cogent document. The learned Subordinate Judge believed the title deeds of the plaintiffs and arrived at the conclusion that the plaintiffs have right, title and interest in the disputed land and they acquired it from their father Khalilur Rahman by way of inheritance and by amicable arrangement with their other co-sharers. The learned Subordinate Judge held also, that when a properly framed title suit has been filed in respect of the same land and when the matter is under investigation in a civil court, the opinions and observation of the Revenue officer was not of much value for the determination of the dispute between the parties. The learned Subordinate Judge also recorded the finding that in the proceeding under section 145 of the Code of Criminal Procedure the possession of the disputed land was found with the First Party Nabibur Rahman Chowdhury (plaintiff No.1) and it was ordered that he would not be disturbed in his possession therein until evicted in due course of law and the Second party, the present defendant No. 1 having not filed a suit for recovery of khas possession within 3 years from the date of the order. The plaintiffs acquired a good title to the property under section 28 of the Limitation Act. The learned Subordinate Judge was of the view that the possibility of dispossession of the plaintiffs by the defendant No. 1 from the suit land after the judgment passed in favour but in view of the facts and circumstances of the case learned Subordinate Judge found that the plaintiff''s suit is not barred by Limitation and reversed the decision of the learned trial judge on the question of limitation allowed the appeal and decreed the suit.

9. Feeling aggrieved by aforesaid decision of the learned Subordinate Judge, the defendant No. 1 preferred this appeal before that Court.

10. The appellant is represented by the learned Advocate Mr BK Das with the learned Advocate Ms Sucharita Sen Gupta. Mr MA Rashid learned Advocate though, appeared and filed power on behalf of the respondent Nos. 1-3 did not appear in the appeal when the same was taken up for hearing although the matter appeared in the list on a good number of days.

11. Since both the courts below concurrently found title of the suit land with the plaintiffs and the same having been concluded by concurrent finding of fact. Mr. B K Das, learned Advocate appearing in support of the appeal with all fairness did not challenge concurrent findings of fact on the question of title decided in favour of the plaintiffs and against the defendant No. 1.

12. Mr BK Das, learned Advocate directed his efforts to assail the decision of the lower appellate Court raising the contention that the finding of possession and limitation arrived at by the lower appellate Court is based purely on a judgment passed by a Magistrate in a proceeding under section 145 of the Criminal Procedure Code deciding factum of possession in favour of the plaintiffs who were first party in the said proceeding. Judgments of criminal courts are not admissible in evidence and also cannot be gone into in deciding question of title in civil proceedings, Mr Das, further, submitted.

13. The next contention on behalf of the appellant is that the plaintiff''s suit falls under Article 142 of the Limitation Act and having onus was on the plaintiffs to prove possession within 12(twelve) years prior to the institution of the suit but the plaintiffs failed to discharge this onus and the lower appellate Court to decide this material point in reversing the decisions of the trial Court failed and the same is not a proper judgment of reversal.

14. Let me now advert to the contention pressed into service from the side of the appellant. Admittedly 0.35 acres of CS Dag No. 2943 corresponding to Survey Settlement Dag No.381 is the suit land. It is the case of the plaintiff that the said CS Dag No. 2943 belonged to their father Khalilur Rahman Chowdhury and the said plot was recorded in his name in the CS of 1331 BS Exhibit 5 and 5(a) are the two CS Record of Rights. Exhibit 5 is the CS Record of Right which is in respect of Dag No. 145 of chelte of 1318 BS and Exhibit 5(a) is CS Record of Right which is in respect of Dag No. 146 and 147 of Chelta of 1331 BS. Exhibits 5 and 5(a) suggest that CS Plot No. 2943 appertained to Taluk No. 6299/20 Lal Mohammad and the same belonged to Khalilur Rahamn Chowdhury, the predecessor father of the plaintiffs. It is the assertion of the defendant that the CS Plot No. 2943 appertained to Taluk No. 702/29 Patta Md Afsar and the same belonged to Obaidur Rahman Chowdhury and the defendant No.1 is alleged to have taken settlement from the landlord Obaindur Rahman Chowdhury. Both the courts below concurrently found that CS Plot No. 2943 appertained to Taluk No.6299/20 Lal Mohammad and not to Taluk No. 702/29 Patta Md Afsar and the same belonged to Khalilur Rahman Chowdhury who was inherited by the plaintiffs along with other co-sharers. So, it is evidently clear that the plaintiffs are the owners of the suit land. The sheet anchor of the defendant''s claim, the alleged settlement of the suit land from Obaidur Rahman Chowdhury fall to the ground. The claim of the defendant of exercising acts of possession on the suit land for the last 35 years on the basis of the said settlement got no foundation at all.

15. The plaintiffs case is of possession and subsequent dispossession. The plaintiff''s suit thus, squarely falls under Article 142 of the Limitation Act. Article 142 of the Limitation Act enjoins that for a suit of possession of immoveable property when the plaintiff while in possession of the property has been dispossessed or has discontinued possession limitation is twelve (12) years from the date of dispossession or discontinuance. Under Article 142 the plaintiff must prove dispossession from or discontinuance of possession of immoveable property within twelve years preceding the date of the suit. Now it is to be seen how far the plaintiffs could prove that their suit was within twelve (12) years from the alleged date of dispossession and the suit is not barred by limitation. It is also not to be evidenced that, there is also an onus on the part of the defendant to prove his possession over the suit land for a period covering 35 years.

16. The plaintiff examined 3 witnesses including plaintiff No. 1 as PW 1. Defendant No.1 examined himself as DW 1 as the sole witness. The trial Court discarded the testimony of PW 1 on the ground that he is a vitally interested witness. The testimony of the PW 2 was also discarded by the trial Court taking the ground that he was friendly with the plaintiffs and so he was interested witness. Similarly, the trial Court also discarded the evidence of PW 3 for his alleged incompetency to prove the factum of possession and dispossession. The trial Court did not at all discuss the evidence of DW 1 who was defendant No. 1 himself. It is well recognized that mere relationship can never be a ground to discard the testimony of a witness unless the same is characterized by internal marks of falsehood. The trial Court did not discard the testimony of the PWs on the ground that their evidences suffered from internal marks of falsehood.

<u>17. The lower appellate Court as final and last court of fact, though, was required to discuss the evidences of the parties, more so, when it was reversing the decisions of the trial Court on the question of possession and limitation did not at all discuss the evidences of the parties. The lower appellate Court rested his decision on Exhibit 3(a), a judgment of a criminal court wherein, in a proceeding under section 145 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, the possession with respect to the suit land was found in favour of the plaintiffs (First party in the said proceeding). The decision of the lower appellate Court on this pertinent question appears to have suffered from patent illegality. Equally the decision on the question of possession arrived at by the trial Court appears to have been based on mere suspicion, surmises and conjectures and the findings to the effect that the defendant was supported by any evidences of record. From the discussions made above it becomes evidently clear that both the courts below misdirected in their approach of the matter and committed a substantial error in the decisions. Faced with this situation I feel inclined to express my view that though it is a case of remand but since 28 years had already passed since the institution of the suit on 1-2-1989, I am not desirous to send the suit/appeal back on remand for fresh decision either by the lower appellate Court or by the trial Court and I like to dispose of the appeal on the basis of evidences and materials on record to which I am permitted under the provision of section 103 of the Code of Civil Procedure.</u>

18. Section 100, 101, 102 and 103 were omitted by the Law Reforms Ordinance, 1978 (Ordinance No. XLIX of 1978) with effect from June 1, 1979 vide Notification published in the Bangladesh Gazette Extraordinary dated 25-4-1978. The said sections remained as existing laws when this second appeal under section 100 of the Code was presented on 13-9-1977.

Section 100 runs thus:

"100.—(1) Save where otherwise expressly provided in the body of this Code or by any other law for the time being in force, an appeal shall lie to the High Court from every decree passed in appeal by any court subordinate to the High Court Division, on any of the following grounds, namely:

(a)	the decision being contrary to law or to some usage having the force of law:

(b)	the decision having failed to determine some material issue of law or usage having the force of law;

(c)	a substantial error or defect in the procedure provided by this Code or by any other law for the time being in force, which may possibly have produced error or defect in the decision of the case upon the merits.

(2) An appeal may lie under this section from an appellate decree passed ex-parte."

Section 103 reads thus:

"103. In any second appeal, the High Court Division may, if the evidence on the record is sufficient, determine any issue of fact necessary for the disposal of the appeal which has not been determined by the lower appellate Court or which has been wrongly determined by such Court by reason of any illegality, omission, error or defect such as is refereed to in sub-section (1) of Section 100."

<u>19. Section 103 as stood before the law Reforms Ordinance of 1978 empowered the High Court Division to come to a finding of fact on the evidences on record where the conditions set out in the aforesaid section are fulfilled and the High Court Division instead of sending the suit/appeal back on remand must take recourse to this section and dispose of the second appeal finally.</u>

20. Turning to the question as to whether the plaintiffs could prove possession within 12 years prior to the filing of the suit I am to advert to the evidences of both PWs and DW 1. Before that relevant paragraph No.8 of the plaint may profitably be extracted which are as follows:

“৮। উল্লেখিত সন ১৯৬২ ইংরেজীর ২৫ নং Special appeal এর রায় বিগত ৩১-৫-৬৬ ইংরেজী তারিখে প্রকাশিত হয়। ঐ রায় বিবাদীর স্বপক্ষে থাকায় মামলাবাজ ১নং মূল বিবাদী ঐ রায়ের বলে উৎসাহিত হইয়া বাদীপক্ষে ১নং বাদীর নিষেধ বাধা অমান্যে বাদীগণের স্বত্ব অস্বীকারে বিগত সন ১৩৭৩ বাংলার পৌষ মাসের মধ্যভাগে নালিশী ভূমিতে অনধিকার প্রবেশে তাহাতে বোরো ধান্য রোপন ক্রমে তাহা হইতে বাদীগণকে বেদখল ক্রমে অদ্যাপি তাহাতে দখলকার আছে। তৎপূর্বে বিবাদী নালিশা ভূমি কখনও দখল করে নাই এবং করার কোন কারণ বা অধিকার ছিল না।”

21. Plaintiff No.1 Nabibur Rahman Chowdhury as PW 1 gave testimony to the effect that they themselves grew paddy on the suit land through servant and thereafter through bargadar and defendant No.1 amalgamated the suit land with his land which lay towards the west. The relevant portion of the evidence is quoted thus "First we ourselves grew paddy therein through servant and later through bargadar. He (defendant No.1) amalgamated the suit land with his land which lies towards the west." On perusal of the cross-examination it does not appear that PW 1 was cross-examined an the statement that the defendant No.1 amalgamated the suit land with his land. PW 2 Samawar Ali testified that he had been sowing the suit land for 23 to 24 years and the suit land was in possession of the plaintiffs. He stated that he bhag cultivated the suit land on behalf of the plaintiffs and the suit land is now in the possession of defendant No.1 for 6/7 years. He further gave testimony that the defendant dispossessed the plaintiffs thereform 6/7 years ago in the month of Poush by planting paddy plant therein and before this dispossession, defendant did not ever possess the suit land. In his cross-examination PW 2 denied the suggestion put forward by the defendant that the plaintiffs are not the owner of the suit land and also that he did not bhag cultivate the suit land. He asserted that defendant No.1 had been possessing the suit land for 7/8 years. This witness correctly stated the area of the land. PW 3 Mahmat Ali gave testimony that he knows the suit land. Further testimony is that the defendant No.1 had been possessing the suit land for 7 to 8 years and he did not know who possessed the suit land before Monohar (Defendant No. 1). The cross-examination of this PW 3 had been declined by the defendant side. Defendant No.1 Monohar Ali as DW 1 gave testimony to the effect that Obaidur Rahman Chowdhury was the owner of the suit land and he took settlement from him 30/31 years ago and he paid him rent and since settlement he had been possessing the suit land. He further testified that the suit land appertained to PS Dag No.381. He further stated that to the north south and west of the suit land is his land and to the east of the suit land is the land of Nabibur Rahman, (plaintiff No.1). He also testified that during his 35 years of possession of the suit land none interrupted him. But there was no testimony by DW 1 to the effect that he did not dispossess the plaintiffs in the middle part of the month of Poush, 1373 BS as alleged by the plaintiffs in paragraph No.8 of the plaint.

<u>22. It had already been pointed out that in paragraph No.8 of the plaint it has been stated that the defendant in the middle part of the month of Poush, 1373 BS dispossessed the plaintiffs. The plaintiff No.1 as PW 1 gave evidence that the defendant No.1amalgamated the suit land with his land. PW 2 gave evidence that the suit land was in possession of the plaintiffs and he bhag cultivated the suit land under the plaintiffs and the suit land was under the possession of the defendant No.1 for 6/7 years and the defendant dispossessed the plaintiffs therefrom 6/7 years ago in the month of Poush, 1373 BS. The PW 3, though, stated that the defendant No. 1 had been possessing the suit land for 7/9 years but he did not know who possessed the suit land before the defendant No.1, possessed the suit land 7-8 years back. The claim of possession and the subsequent dispossession of the plaintiffs on the suit land appears to have been established by PW 1 and PW 2 even if the testimony of PW 3 is left out from consideration. It is significant to notice that defendant No. 1, though specifically pleaded of his possession over the suit land for 35 years the alleged possession was not at all corroborated by any evidence whatsoever. Without any corroboration it is difficult to accept the contention of the defendant that he was in possession of the suit land for the last 35 years specially when the foundation of his possession ie the alleged settlement from landlord Obaidur Rahman Chowdhury with respect to Taluk No.702/29 fall to the ground. Law is settled that possession always follows from lawful title. In this case the title of the suit land was not found with the defendant No. 1 and the same was found with the plaintiffs by both the courts below. The defendant No. 1 in the written statement and as well as in the evidence set out the case that he got possession over the suit land for about 35 years back from Obaidur Rahman Chowdhury on the basis of a settlement from him and no case had been set up that the defendant No.1 forcibly entered into possession on the suit land in total denial of the right, title, interest and possession of the plaintiffs and the possession was notorious and hostile and as such the question of acquisition of title by adverse possession did not and does not arise. In support of the contention on behalf of the appellant that the plaintiffs having signally failed to prove their possession within 12 years of the institution of the suit, the same stood barred by limitation, reliance has been placed on Ahmed Miaji and others vs Eakub Ali Munshi and others, 12 DLR HC 708, Arabjan Bibi vs Abdul Kadid and others, 19 DLR 743, Syed Main Ahmed vs Kh Mohiuddin, 19 DLR 912; Raman Ali alias Md Rakman Ali and others vs Hasib Ali Chowdhury and others, 24 DLR 146. The judicial views emerging out of the authorities refered to above is that where plaintiff pleads possession and dispossession, the onus is upon him to prove such possession and dispossession and the case will be controlled by Article 142 of the Limitation Act.</u>

<u>23. The proposition of law enunciated in the aforesaid authorities is not at all disputed. On a perusal of the pleading and a careful analysis and appraisement of the evidence and materials brought on record it is seen that the plaintiffs could prove their possession and subsequent dispossession on the suit land and the suit was filed within 12 years of the date of dispossession and the suit is not barred by limitation. I do not find any substance in the appeal. The appeal, thus, fails.</u>

24. In the result, the appeal is dismissed, however without any order as to cost. The judgment and decree of the lower appellate Court are maintained though not for the reasons stated in the said judgment.

Send down the LC Record at once.

End.

caseno: Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No. 681 of 2009.

Vs

case_source: (From the judgment and order dated 15-1-2009 passed by the High Court Division in Civil Revision No. 1396 of 2007).
full_judgment:
Syed Mahmud Hossain J: This civil petition for leave to appeal is directed against the judgment and order dated 15-1-2009 passed by a Single Bench of the High Court Division in Civil Revision No. 1396 of 2007 discharging the Rule and affirming the judgment and order dated 7-3-2007 passed by the learned District Judge, Bogra in Civil Revision No. 98 of 2006 reversing the order dated 27-7-2006 passed by the learned Senior Assistant Judge, Bogra in Other Suit No.300 of 2000 allowing an application under Order VI, rule 17 of the Code of Civil Procedure.

2. The facts, leading to the filing of this petition, in brief, are that the petitioners and others instituted Other Suit No. 300 of 2000 in the Court of Senior Assistant Judge, First Court, Bogra for declaration of their easement right to the suit ponds. Their case, in short, is that during the CS operation the suit ponds were recorded in the name of Bharat Samrat and the names of Gyanoda Prashad Sukul, Chandra Prashad Sukul and Jogodeshwari Debba were recorded as the possessors who had been enjoying the possession thereof on payment of rent to the concerned authority. After the death of those persons, the petitioners perform a respondents and the villagers of the respective villages had been enjoying the possession of the suit ponds claiming their easement right. The suit pond measuring 1.93 acres appertaining to CS Khatian No.17 containing Plot No. 709 belonged to one Jogodeshwari and others. In the remark's column of the said khatian that pond had been shown as being used 'by the public' but in the DP Khatian No.1362 the said pond had been wrongly recorded in the name of respondent No.2 having no right, title, interest and possession therein. The suit pond measuring 1.71 acres of plot No. 680 appertaining to CS khatian No. 17 is being used by the public but in the DP Khatian No. 538 the same had been wrongly recorded in the name of respondent No. 1. The suit pond measuring 0.23 acre of CS Khatian No. 17 containing plot No. 1108 belonged to Jogodeshwari and others and the said pond is also being used by the public but in DP Khatian No.1076 the same had been wrongly recorded in the name of respondent Nos. 3-5. It has further been alleged that the defendants-respondents in connivance with the settlement officials have managed to get their names recorded in DP Khatian in respect of the suit ponds. In fact, the petitioners and the general public have been enjoying the possession of the said ponds in exercise of their easement right. The cause of action of the suit arose on 15-11-2000 when the defendants-respondents obstructed the petitioners from exercising their right of easement in the suit ponds. Hence the suit.

3. The defendants respondents appeared and contested the suit by filing a joint written statement denying the materials statements made in the plaint.

<u>4. On 16-5-2006, the petitioners filed an application under Order VI, rule 17 of the Code of Civil Procedure before the learned Senior Assistant Judge, First Court, Bogra for amendment of the plaint. They stated, inter alia, that owing to inadvertence some important facts have not been incorporated in the plaint. Not only correction of the description of the names of some of the plaintiffs is necessary but striking out the name of plaintiff No. 61 is also essential. Inclusion of CS Khatian No.18 containing plot Nos.709, 680 and 1108 essential and a paragraph to the effect that the plaintiffs-petitioners shall conduct the suit in representative character for declaration of their easement and customary right on replacing the original prayer for declaration of their title over the suit ponds is also necessary.</u>

5. Respondent Nos.1-13 contested the application by filing written objection dated 28-6-2006. They contended, inter alia, that the proposed amendment has introduced new facts and different cause of action from those which have been made earlier in the plaint and that the said prayer has been made after 6(six) years from the date of initiation of the instant suit. It has been contended that the procedures under Order I, rule 8 of the Code of Civil Procedure having not been complied with, the prayer for amendment of the plaint should be rejected.

6. The learned Senior Assistant Judge, First Court, Bogra by his judgment and order dated 27-7-2006 allowed the application.

7. Being aggrieved respondent Nos.1-13 preferred Civil Revision No. 98 of 2006 before the District Judge, Bogra who after hearing both the parties, vide judgment and order dated 7-3-2007 allowed the said Civil Revision setting aside the order dated 27-7-2006 passed by the learned Senior Assistant Judge, First Court, Bogra in Other Suit No. 300 of 2000.

8. Challenging the judgment and order passed by the learned District Judge rejecting the prayer for amendment the plaintiffs-petitioners filed a revisional application before the High Court Division and obtained Rule in Civil Revision No.1396 of 2007.

9. The High Court Division discharged the Rule by the impugned judgment and order dated 15-1-2009.

10. Feeling aggrieved by and dissatisfied with the judgment and order passed by the High Court Division, the plaintiffs-petitioners have preferred this civil petition for leave to Appeal before this Division.

<u>11. Mr. Shaheed Alam, learned Advocate, appearing on behalf of the leave petitioners, submits that the High Court Division wrongly came to a finding that the proposed amendment would change nature and character of the suit although addition of new fact cannot in any way change the nature and character and, as such, the impugned judgment delivered by the High Court Division should be set aside.</u>

12. Mr. Abul Kalam Mainuddin, learned Advocate appearing on behalf of respondent Nos.1-13, supports the impugned judgment and order passed by the High Court Division.

13. We have considered the submissions of the learned Advocates, the impugned judgment and order and the materials on record.

<u>14. The plaintiffs instituted Other Class Suit No. 300 of 2000 in the Court of Senior Assistant Judge, First Court, Bogra, for declaration of title and for establishment of their easement right over the suit ponds. From the impugned judgment, it appears that the plaintiffs amended the plaint more than once. On 15-6-2006, the plaintiffs filed an application under Order VI, rule 17 read with section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure for amendment of plaint incorporating new facts and prayer.</u>

15. On 27-7-2006, the trial Court allowed the application for amendment of plaint with a cost of Tk.500 as it was filed at a belated stage without assigning any other reason whatsoever.

<u>16. The contesting defendant challenged the order of amendment in Civil Revision No. 98 of 2006 before the District Judge, Bogra. On 7-3-2007, the learned District Judge allowed the revision holding that in the application, it was not clarified as to why the application for amendment was filed at a belated stage and that the amendment had changed the nature and character of the suit.</u>

17. The High Court Division affirmed the judgment and order of the learned District Judge holding that the amendment would change the nature and character of the suit.

<u>18. Having considered the application for amendment, it appears that the plaintiffs incorporated new facts by the amendment but incorporation of new fact cannot in any way change the nature and character of the suit. The suit still be named as a suit for declaration of plaintiffs' easement right. The finding of the High Court Division that the nature and character of the suit would be changed by the amendment without elaboration of its finding cannot sustain in law. Amendment is always necessary to determine the real question of controversy between the parties, otherwise there is likelihood of cropping-up of multifarious litigations.</u>

<u>19. Admittedly the trial Court allowed the application for amendment by a cryptic and slipshod order. A judicial order devoid of reasoning causes error of law but mere error of law cannot be a ground for interference unless it has occasioned failure of justice. While exercising any discretion under Order VI, rule 17 of the Code of Civil Procedure the Court is required to assign its reasons so that when the order is called in question, the higher Court may be in position to see that there has been application of mind by the Court concerned and that it is aware of the principles involved in the exercise of its discretion.</u>

20. In this connection, reliance may made on the case of Abdul Motaleb vs Md. Ershad Ali, 18 BLD (AD)121= 4 BLC (AD) 150 in which it was held that, since the impugned order was not a speaking order, could not by itself be a valid ground for interference by the High Court Division unless it could be shown that the Subordinate Court has committed any error of law 'resulting in an error in the decision occasioning failure of justice'. The order of the learned Senior Assistant Judge may have been a bad or improper order for not assigning reasons but before interfering with the same the High Court Division is required to examine whether the same has resulted in an erroneous decision occasioning failure of justice.

21. In the above case, the Appellate Division held as under:-

"There is one limitation in amending a plaint which is well recognized, that is, the nature and character of a suit cannot be changed by amendment. It is not, however, always correctly appreciated as to what is meant by a change in the nature and character of the suit. For example, as in the present case, a simple suit for declaration of title to the suit land was converted following an alleged dispossession in the meantime, into a suit for recovery of possession by amendment. Can it be said that by adding a new prayer for recovery of possession there has been a change, although apparently it may seem so, in the nature and character of the suit? 'The answer is obviously no. Has there been a change in the nature and character of the suit then by adding the prayer for partition which was allowed by the learned Subordinate Judge? The answer again must be no, because the principle is that the nature and character of a suit do not change so long as the fundamental character of the suit remains the same."

<u>22. In the above case, this Division has found that a suit for simple declaration of title to the suit land may continue with an additional prayer for recovery if the dispossession was made during pendency of the suit. Even in a suit for declaration of title and recovery of possession, the plaintiff may ask for partition and such amendment by introducing a relief for partition will not change the nature and character of the suit.</u>

23. In the case of Managing Committee NMC Model High School vs Obaidur Rahman Chowdhury 31 DLR (AD) 133, the plaintiff initially filed a suit for permanent injunction. During progress of the suit the defendants raised some structures and then the plaintiff filed an application under Order VI, rule 17 of the Code of Civil Procedure praying for amendment of plaint by adding a new prayer for declaration of title and recovery of possession of a portion alleged to have been encroached upon by the defendants. The plaintiffs paid advalorem court fee on the proposed amended plaint. The order of amendment was upheld by the Courts below. Turning down the contention of the defendants who stated that the proposed amendment would change the nature and character of the suit land this Division held as under:—

"Turning to the leave order we find that it is now well-settled that the amendment of the pleadings could be allowed at any stage of the proceedings for the purpose of determining the real question of controversy between the parties, but it could not be allowed, if, it changed the nature and character of the suit, or if the prayer for amendment had became barred by lapse of time and a right had accrued to the other side. But the latter principle can be departed from, if there are circumstances which outweigh the hardship and cause a prejudice to the applicant."

24. In the case referred to above this Division relied upon the case of Charan Das vs Amir Khan, AIR 1921 PC 50, which has been followed by the Supreme Court of Pakistan in the case of Keramat Ali vs Muhammad Younus Haji PLD 1963 (SC) 191=15 DLR (SC) 120. This Division also considered the case of Md. Zahoor Ali Khan's case 11 MLA 468 in which Privy Council's observation is that the Mufussil Court's pleadings are to be construed liberally and for the confused pleadings, the party should not suffer. We cannot make ourselves oblivious of the prevailing situation in the Mufussil Courts where drafting of good pleading is a rarity now-a-days. For the failure of the lawyers the common litigants should not be penalized. One of the fundamental principles governing the amendment of the pleadings is that all the controversies between the parties as far as possible should be included and multiplicity of the proceedings avoided.

25. Therefore, the judgment and order passed by the High Court Division affirming the judgment and order passed by the learned District Judge cannot sustain.

26. Admittedly the suit filed in 2000 is yet to be disposed of by the trial Court. Such being the state of affairs we do not find any point dragging the case before this Division in an interlocutory matter. Therefore, it would be proper to dispose of this Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal.

Accordingly the impugned judgment and order passed by the Court Division affirming the judgment and order passed by the learned District Judge is set aside and the order of trial Court allowing amendment is restored. The trial Court is directed to dispose of the suit as expeditiously as possible.

End.

case_source: (From the judgment and order 3-10-2007 passed by the High Court Division in Civil Revision No.1887 of 1990 heard analogously with Civil Revision No.1888 of 1990).
full_judgment:
Md Abdul Matin J : These petitions for leave to appeal are directed against the judgment and order dated 3-10-2007 passed by the High Court Division in Civil Revision No. 1887 of 1990 heard analogously with Civil Revision No. 1888 of 1990 discharging the Rule arising out of judgment and decree dated 5-4-1990 and 26-5-1990 respectively passed by the learned Subordinate Judge, Narail in Title Appeal No. 64 of 1987 dismissing the Appeal of the petitioner and affirming the judgment and decree passed by the learned Assistant Judge, Narail in Title Suit No.383 of 1978.

2. The facts, in short, are that the petitioner as a plaintiff filed Title Suit No. 383 of 1978 in the Court of learned Assistant Judge, Narail for declaration of her title to the suit property contending, inter alia, that the said property originally belonged to Sukumar Bose and others. In a partition suit being Partition Suit No. 132 of 1967 in the 3rd Court of Munsif, Narail the respondent opposite party No. 6 got the said property on the basis of a compromise decree passed in the said suit on 23-1-1968 and thereafter sold the present suit premise to the plaintiff-petitioner by a Saf-kabala deed dated 21-1-1974 and handed over peaceful vacant possession of the said properties to her and since then she is in possession of the same in exercising her exclusive right, title and interest in respect thereof, that while the plaintiff-petitioner had been enjoying the schedule property in the said manner one of her relations namely, Dr Raj Kumar Kundu (now deceased) the predecessor of the defendant-opposite party Nos.2-5, requested the plaintiff-petitioner for temporary shelter to reside in the suit property, specially in the suit buildings consisting of five rooms including kitchen. Being thus requested the appellant-petitioner allowed the said Dr Raj Kumar Kundu, the predecessor of the respondent-opposite party Nos. 2-5, to make temporary use of the suit premises as their residence as licensees, that since then the said Raj Kumar Kundu including the respondent-opposite party Nos. 2-5 are residing there as licensees holding permissive possession from the appellant-petitioner of the said suit premises. On 30-5-1978 one of the employees of the respondent-opposite party No.1 informed the husband of appellant-petitioner that the property in question had been placed in the vested property list and the same would be leased out. The further contention of the appellant-petitioner is that the schedule properties could not be a vested property under any circumstances as she had been enjoying and possessing the same by purchase and had mutated her name in the record of right and had been paying the rents to the Government regularly, that her vendor Probhabati Dasi, the respondent-opposite party No. 6, is a Bangladeshi citizen and therefore the property in question is the legally acquired property of her own. The contention of respondent-opposite party No. 1 regarding vested property is false and without lawful authority and, as such, the appellant-petitioner was constrained to file the suit.

3. The case of the respondent-defendant No.1 is that the previous owner of the suit property left for India before 1965 and since then they were residing there as Indian Nationals and that the property in question naturally is a vested and non-resident one, the defendant Nos. 3-6 are unauthorised occupiers having no right, title and interest therein.

4. The case of respondent-opposite party Nos.2-5 was that their father, Raj Kumar Kundu, was a physician who used to practice at Rupganj Bazar whereat he had a dispensary. The said Raj Kumar Kundu desired to purchase a property for his residential purpose. Sukumar Bose, the owner of the suit premises, offered to sell the same and the price having been fixed at Taka 3,000 (Taka three thousand) a sum of Taka 1,500 (one thousand five hundred) only had been paid to Sukumar Bose by the said Raj Kumar Kundu as earnest money in the year 1952 and the possession of the suit property was handed over to the vendee by the vendor and since then they are in possession of the suit property. On 7-4-1962 their father, Raj Kumar Kundu paid up the balance consideration money of Taka 1,500 (Taka one thousand five hundred) to Sukumar Bose and on the same date a written agreement was made between the parties. The said Sukumar Bose thereafter left for India for his treatment and died there. Thereafter the father of the respondent-opposite party Nos. 2-5 died, that they could not know about the alleged decree in Title Suit No. 132 of 1967. Sukumar Bose having not been residing at Machimdia in the year 1967 could not make any solenama as alleged by the plaintiff-appellant petitioner. The alleged solenama decree of said title suit is false, fabricated, concocted and obtained by practising fraud upon the Court. Probhabati had no right, title, interest and possession of the suit property and the alleged "Saf-Kabala" deed was forged, fictitious and without any consideration. The plaintiff-appellant petitioner did not possess the suit property at any point of time and respondent-opposite party Nos. 2-5 did not have any permissive possession under plaintiff-appellant petitioner. The further contention of the respondent opposite party Nos. 2-5 is that the respondent-opposite party No. 1 having treated them as unauthorised occupiers in the suit premises and the property in question having been declared as vested property clouds have been cast upon the right, title and interest of their property in question hence, they have been constrained to file Title Suit No. 623 of 1979 in the Court of learned Assistant Judge, Narail for declaration of their title.

<u>5. The trial Court dismissed the Title Suit No. 383 of 1978 and decreed the Title Suit No. 623 of 1979 in favour of the present respondent and declared that the defendant Nos. 2-5 acquired ownership of the suit house by adverse possession and they are entitled to retain their possession of the same. On appeal the appellate Court affirmed the judgment and decree of the trial Court and dismissed the appeal and the High Court Division on revision affirmed the judgment of the courts below and discharged the Rule.</u>

6. Heard the learned Advocate and perused the petition and the impugned judgment and order of the High Court Division and other papers on record.

<u>7. It appears that both the trial Court and the court of appeal concurrently held that the plaintiff could not produce the sole decree passed in Partition Suit No.132 of 1967 and could not prove the basis of acquisition of title by Probhabati Debi and therefore did not acquire any title by the alleged purchase from Probhabati Debi by Exhibit 1 and therefore, the High Court Division was right in affirming the judgment of the Courts below.</u>

<u>We find no merit in these petitions which are accordingly, dismissed.</u>

End.

Abdul Quayum with Probir Halder and Swarup Kanti Deb, Advocates—For the Petitioner.

full_judgment:
Farid Ahmed J: This Rule was issued calling upon the opposite parties to show cause as in why the impugned order No. 20 dated 3-7-2006 passed by the learned Joint District Judge, 1st Court, Khulna in entertaining the Miscellaneous Case No. 24 of 2006 under Order IX, rule 13 should not be set aside and or such other or further order or orders passed as to this Court may seem fit and proper.

2. The petitioner on 1-8-2005 instituted Money Suit No. 6 of 2005 before the 1st Court of Joint District Judge, Khulna against the opposite parties for a decree for Taka 53,97,3,000 as compensation for damage and for mandatory injunction directing the defendant-opposite parties to hand over key of chamber of the factory and to restrain them from interfering in the running of the business of the plaintiff-petitioner namely 'Rupsha Fish and Allied Industries'.

3. The learned Court by order dated 11-9-2005 fixed up 18-10-2005 for filing written statements and thereafter consecutively on 4 dates the defendant-opposite parties failed to file written statements. The learned Joint District Judge by order No. 12 dated 22-1-2006 as last chance allowed time and fixed up 6-2-2006 for filing written statements with a cost of Taka 700, in default, for ex parte hearing and decision. On 6-2-2006 the defendants appointed a new lawyer and again filed an application for 15 days adjournment to file written statements. The Court rejected the prayer for adjournment and took up the case for ex parte hearing and decreed the suit ex parte.

4. Against the said ex parte decree the defendant opposite parties have filed a case being Miscellaneous Case No. 24 of 2006 under Order IX, rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure stating that defendant-opposite parties could not prepare the written statements as the Head Office of the Bards did not supply the necessary facts and documents in support of their case and that they engaged a new Advocate but he could not prepare the written statements and, as such, prayed for time, the learned Court rejected the prayer for time and passed the ex parte decree. In the miscellaneous case the petitioner filed an application stating that the impugned ex parte order was passed under Order VIII, rule 10 of the Code of Civil Procedure which is appealable, so, the miscellaneous petition under Order IX, rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure is not maintainable.

5. The learned Joint District Judge by order No. 20 dated 3-7-2006 rejected the application for rejection of the miscellaneous case on the finding that in order to avoid delay and for expeditious disposal of the case the provision of rule 13(A) of Order IX has been inserted in the Code of Civil Procedure.

6. Being aggrieved thereby, the petitioner moved this Court and obtained the present Rule.

7. The defendant-opposite parties have filed a counter-affidavit controverting the statements made in the revisional application and stated that in their miscellaneous case they stated that for bonafide reason they failed to file written statements within the time granted by the Court and that as per provision of rule 13A of Order IX of the Civil Procedure Code, to ensure the expeditious hearing of the case the learned Court rejected the petitioner's application for rejection of the miscellaneous case and that the said miscellaneous case is maintainable.

8. Mr Abdul Quayum with Mr Probir Halder, learned Advocates appearing on behalf of petitioner-company have submitted that the ex parte order was passed as per provision of Order VIII, rule 10 which is appealable under Order XLI rule 1(3) of the Code of Civil Procedure and, as such, the miscellaneous case is not maintainable. Mr. Probir Halder thereafter has submitted that petitioner took specific ground that an appeal lies against the order passed under Order VIII, rule 10 of the Code of Civil Procedure and the learned Judge quoted the submission of the petitioner in his judgment but without considering the said provision of law illegally rejected the petitioner's application for rejection of the miscellaneous case.

9. Mr. Ajmalul Hossain, learned Senior Counsel appearing with Mr. ABM Siddiqur Rahman Khan and Mr Mamun Chowdhury learned Advocates, have submitted that the order passed by the Joint District Judge in the money suit is an ex parte decree within the meaning of Order IX, rule 6 of the CPC and, as such, an application under Order IX, rule 13 of the CPC is attracted. Mr Ajmalul Hossain thereafter has submitted that the judgment passed in the money suit deemed to be a decree under Order XVII, rule 2 of the CPC and the remedy lies under Order IX, rule 13 of the CPC. He further has submitted that 1st part of the Order IX, rule 13 of the CPC defines that in case of every ex parte decree an application under Order IX, rule 13 is maintainable and the present miscellaneous case being an application against the ex parte decree under the 2nd limb of the Order VIII, rule 10 the proper forum is an application under Order IX, rule 13 of the CPC. He lastly has submitted that the ex parte judgment passed in the Money suit being not a judgment within the meaning of section 2(9) and Order XX, rule 4 of the CPC the application under Order IX, rule 13 is entertain able.

10. Certified copy of the entire order sheet of the Money Suit No. 6 of 2005 has been annexed with the revisional application as Annexure-B. From order No. 12 dated 22-1-2006 it appears that previously on 4 occasions adjournments were allowed for filing written statements but the defendant did not file any written statements. The Court by that order again granted adjournment for the last time and fixed up 6-2-2006 for filing written statements with a cost of Taka 700, in default, fixed for ex parte disposal and decision of the case. The defendants without filing any written statements and without depositing the cost money filed an application for time to file written statements. This application was filed by a new lawyer who stated that the previous lawyer of the defendants retired from the case. The defendants then and there deposited the cost amount and made a prayer for adjournment. The learned Court rejected the said prayer and took up the case for ex parte hearing and disposed of the case by an ex parte judgment.

11. The learned Advocate for the opposite party has submitted that the ex parte decree was passed in absence of the learned Advocate and that the learned Court debarred him from appearing in the case. So, the miscellaneous case under Order IX, rule 13 of the CPC is maintainable. In support of his submission he referred three decisions.

12. In the case of Damodar Das vs Raj Kumar Das reported in AIR 1922 (Patna) 485 the suit was decreed ex parte on 20-9-1919. The defendant applied under Order IX, rule 13 of the CPC to have the decree set aside. The High Court found that the trial took place on the 11th, 12th and 13th August, 1919 and on the 11th the defendants' pleader appeared and asked for an adjournment which was refused. He renewed the application on the following day stating that he had no instruction from his client to cross-examine the plaintiff whose evidence had been taken on the 11th. His application was again refused.

13. In the case of Bothra vs Kedar Nath Bothra reported in AIR 1938 (Calcutta) 74 the plaintiffs in the suit at a late stage applied for the issue of a commission. The learned Counsel for the plaintiffs, when the suit was called on, applied for an adjournment, in order that he might be in a position to tender the commission evidence after the commission had been executed. The Court rejected the application. Thereupon Counsel stated that he was not in a position to proceed. The suit was accordingly dismissed. It has been held that if the plaintiff s Counsel confines himself to asking for an adjournment and when it is refused, retires from the case and states that he has no further instruction in that case it cannot be said that in presence of the plaintiff decree was passed.

14. In the case of Md Nurul Haque vs Sonali Bank of Bangladesh reported in 39 DLR 223 their Lordships held:

"………………..It is apparent that after rejection of the prayer for adjournment when the suit was called on for hearing the plain-tiff did not appear within the meaning of Order IX, rule 8 read with Order XVII, rule 2 of the CPC and the learned Subordinate Judge dismissed the suit for default"

15. In all the aforesaid cases there was an application for adjournment which was rejected by the Court. The learned Advocate there-after withdrew him from the suit and intimated the Court that he has no further instruction from his client. So, it was held that the suit was disposed of in absence of the Advocate and miscellaneous case under Order IX, rule 13 were entertained.

<u>16. The ex parte judgment shows that the learned Judge rejected the defendants' application for adjournment and thereafter took up the case for ex parte hearing. It does not appear from the order that the newly appointed lawyer thereafter filed any application for further adjournment or that the learned Advocate intended to appear for taking part in the hearing of the suit. Even he did not retire from the suit.</u>

<u>17. 6-2-2006 was fixed for filing written statements, in default, for taking ex parte derision on the suit. The defendants on that date also failed to file written statements. The learned Court thereafter passed the judgment for failure of the defendants to file written statements. This judgment comes within the purview of Order VIII, rule 10 of the CPC. Order VIII, rule 10 of the Code of Civil Procedure reads as under:</u>

<u>"Where any party from whom a written statement is so required fails to present the same within the time fixed by the Court, the Court may pronounce judgment against him, or make such order in relation to the suit as it thinks fit."</u>

<u>18. So, the order passed by the Court clearly comes within the preview of Order VIII, rule 10 of the CPC. An order passed under Order VIII, rule 10 of the CPC is an appealable order under the provision of Order XLIII, rule 1(b) of the CPC. The provision of Order XLIII, rule 1(b) of the CPC reads as under:</u>

<u>"1. An appeal shall lie from the following order under the provisions of section 104, namely:</u>

<u>(a) ……………………..</u>

<u>(b) an order under Rule 10 of Order VIII pronouncing judgment against a party"</u>

19. According to learned Advocate for the opposite party the impugned judgment having been passed under the provision of Order XVII, rule 2 of the Code of Civil Procedure the application under Order IX, rule 13 is maintainable and that the ex parte judgment passed in money suit can be considered as an order under the second limb of Rule 10 of Order VIII of the Code of Civil Procedure. In case of failure to file written statement the Court can take two courses: (1) pass an ex parte judgment and (2) can make such order in relation to the suit as it thinks fit. In support of his submission he relied on the case of Narendra Patra vs Shiba Narayan Taldi reported in AIR 1995 Orissa 45, Innovation Apartments Flat Owners Association, Secundrabad vs Innovation Associates, Secundrabad reported in AIR 1991 Andhra Pradesh 69, Jayaraman vs Glaxo Laboratories India Ltd reported in AIR 1981 Madras 258, Kuvarp Industries Bangalore vs State Bank of Mysore reported in AIR 1985 (Kant) 77 and the case of MS Manick Peter vs K Surcndra Nathan reported in AIR 1988 Kerala 161. In all these cases it has been decided that an order passed under Order VIII, rule 10 of the Code of Civil Procedure can be challenged by an application under Order IX, rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure.

<u>20. The learned Advocate for the petitioner on the contrary, has submitted that against an order passed under Order VIII, rule 10 of the CPC is appealable under Order XLIII, rule 1(b) of the CPC but in India the provision of Rule 1(b) of Order XLIII of the CPC has been deleted in 1976 by an amendment and there is no provision in the Indian CPC for filing an appeal against the order passed under Order VIII, rule 10 of the CPC. So, in all the aforesaid cases referred on behalf of opposite party it was held that Order IX, rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure is entertain able against an order passed under Order VIII, rule 10 of the CPC. But in our CPC the provision of Rule 1(b) of Order XLIII of the CPC has not been amended. According to our CPC, Rule 1(b) of Order XLIII is the specific provision for filing an appeal against an order passed under Order VIII, rule 10 of the CPC if the defendant fails to present the written statements on the date fixed by the Court. The learned Advocate for the petitioner has referred the case of Gopi Charan Bajpai no Ramprashad Awasthi reported in AIR 1957 (Allahabad) 283. The case was decided before amendment of the CPC in India and it has been held that an order passed under Order VIII, rule 10 of the CPC is an appealable order and appeal lies under the provision of Order XLIII, rule 1(b) of the CPC. Before amendment of CPC in India the provision of Order XLIII, rule 1(b) was the procedure for filing an appeal against an order passed under Order VIII, rule 10 of the CPC. But after amendment the provision of appeal has been deleted in India. In the case of MS Manick Peter no K Surendranathan reported in AIR 1988 Kerala 161 it has been held:</u>

<u>"………………….. A right of appeal provided under Order XLIII, rule 1(b) was taken away by deletion of sub-clause (b). The decree passed in the present case is in conformity with the requirement of Order VIII, rule 10 as amended in 1976. For the absence of the defendants and their Counsel, it is also a decree ex parte. Order IX, rule 13 CPC enables the defendants to apply to the Court to set aside an ex parte decree against him"</u>

21. Mr Probir Holder also referred the case of Hakumat Bibi vs Imam Din reported in PLD 1987 (SC) 22. In that case ex parte decree was passed for not filing the written statements On the date fixed by the Court. An appeal was filed against that order under the provision of Order XLIII, rule 1(b) of the Code of Civil Procedure. In Pakistan the provision of Order XLIII, rule 1(b) neither has been amended nor deleted. The provision of appeal under Order XLIII, rule 1(b) against an order passed under Order VIII, rule 10 still is present in Pakistan like Bangladesh.

22. It has been argued on behalf of opposite parties that the ex parte judgment passed by the lower Court is not a judgment as defined in section 2(9) read with Order XX, rule 4(2) of the Code of Civil Procedure as the learned Court did not consider the case of the parties, the document and the evidence cited by the plaintiff-petition in support of his case. In the case in hand the Court passed a short judgment disposing the suit in favour of plaintiff and did not at all consider the facts of the case and a decree was drawn. As per provision of Rule 10 of Order VIII the Court had two options open to it to deal with the situation arising out of the failure of the opposite party to file written statements despite they having been allowed several opportunities to do so. One of the options was to decide the suit forthwith, (ii) to make such order in relation to the suit as it thought fit. As per the provision of Order VIII, rule 10 the Court can pass a judgment if the defendant fails to file written statements on the date used by the Court. In the present case the judgment passed by the Court is an order and the Court was not required to draw a decree in support of the said judgment. On this point we get support from the case referred by the learned Advocate for the petitioner in the case of Sarder Sakhwat-uddin vs Muhammad iqbal reported in PLD 1983 (Lahore) 448. In that case it was held that "after making the impugned order the learned Senior Civil Judge had drawn up a decree sheet as well. It was perhaps through inadvertence that the decree sheet was prepared because, as held above the order passed by him was an order and not a decree. The mere fact that he had erroneously drawn up the decree sheet would not change the true character of the order under review. In that case the case of the Province of Punjab ruled by the Pakistan SC was considered and wherein it was held:

“………………an order pronouncing the judgment against the defendants for failure to file written statements is an appealable order but not a decree. The use of the ward "Judgment" in rule 10 of Order VIII of the Code of Civil Procedure is of little avail to the respondents because according to the definition of the "Judgment" as given in clause 9 of section 2 of the above Code a decree as well as an order is a judgment. It is therefore, not correct to say that only that adjudication of the Court which is followed by a decree is a judgment and that any other adjudication, though appealable, is not a judgment"

23. The Court has drawn up a decree in terms of the judgment but the same was not necessary and for drawing up such decree it cannot be said that it is a decree within the meaning of section 2(9) of the CPC and the judgment comes within the preview of Order IX, rule 6 of the Code of Civil Procedure and against the said judgment the miscellaneous case under Order IX, rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure is maintainable.

24. Referring the 1st part of the Order IX, rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure the learned Advocate for the opposite party has submitted that in any case in which an ex parte decree is passed against a defendant, he may apply to the Court for setting aside the ex parte decree by an application under Order IX, rule 19 of the CPC. In support of his submission be referred the case of Innovation Apartments Flat Owners Association, Secundrabad vs Innovation Associates Sectindrabad reported in AIR 1991 (Andhra Pradesh) 69. From plain reading of the entire provision of rule 13 of Order IX it appears to as that if the Court is satisfied that the summons was not duly served upon the defendant or that he was prevented by sufficient cause from appearing at the hearing, the Court can set aside an ex parte decree. Specific provision has been made for preferring an appeal under Order XLIII, rule 1(b) of the CPC when an order is passed under Order VIII, rule 10 of the CPC and an application under Order IX, rule 13 will not be entertain able in the garb of "in any case" mentioned in the provision of Order IX, rule 13 of the CPC. Moreover, the decision referred in AIR 1991 (Andhra Pradesh) 69 was passed on 30-8-1990 when the Indian CPC was amended in 1976 and rule 1(b) of Order XLIII was deleted. 'In any case' mentioned in rule 13 of Order IX of the Code of Civil Procedure can only be entertained when it is found is that the summons of the suit was not properly served or that the defendant was prevented by sufficient cause in appearing on the date of hearing of the suit.

25. By amending rule 1 of Order VIII of the CPC provision has been made to file written statement within the time not exceeding two months from the 1st date of hearing. But before amendment there was no specific time limit in the CPC for filing written statement. Before amendment it was in the discretion of the Court to allow time to the defendant to file written statement but after amendment the written statement is required to be filed before the first hearing or within 2 months. The defendants on 11-9-2005, 18-10-2005, 24-11-2005 and 22-1-2006 took four adjournments for filing written statements and the Court by order No. 12 dated 22-1-2006 allowed time with a cost of Taka 700 and directed the defendant to file written statement on 6-2-2006 with a direction that the suit would be taken up for ex parte decision in case of failure of the defendant to file written statement on that date. On the fixed date on 6-2-2006 the defendant appointed a new lawyer who again prayed for time to file written statement. On the previous date they were allowed time to file written statements with cost even then on the next date without filing any written statement they again prayed for adjournment. The defendants had the opportunity to avoid ex parte judgment by filing a written statement with some facts and thereafter they could file additional written statement but the defendant without filing written statements prayed for adjournment, so, the Court did not allow time and proceeded with the ex parte hearing. It does not appear from the order sheet that the learned Advocate thereafter prayed for any adjournment or that he retired from the case. When the Court proceeded for hearing of the case ex parte the learned Advocate for the defendant-opposite party was present in Court but did not take any step. It has been urged that the learned Advocate for the defendant was debarred from appearing in the suit when the some was taken up for hearing but there is no evidence before us to show that learned Advocate of the defendant was not allowed to appear in the suit.

<u>26. From the impugned order it appears that the learned Joint District Judge refused to reject the miscellaneous case on referring the amended provision of rule 13A of Order IX of the CPC. The new provision of rule 13A of Order IX has been brought in the CPC to avoid delay and expedite disposal in setting aside the ex parte decree with cost without requiring the defendant to adduce evidence if an application for setting aside decree is filed within thirty days from the date of decree. But in the present case, the defendant was very much before the Court. He took four adjournments for filing written statements but ultimately they failed to file the same and the Court passed the ex parte judgment which comes within the meaning of Order VIII, rule 10 of the Code of Civil Procedure and the same was appealable under the provision of Order XLIII, rule 1(b) of the Code of Civil Procedure. So, the learned Joint District Judge was not justified in rejecting the petitioner's prayer for rejecting the miscellaneous case as being not entertain able. We find substance in the Rule.</u>

In the result, the Rule is made absolute without any order as to cost. The impugned order No. 20 dated 3-7-2006 is set aside. The miscellaneous case No. 24 of 2006 of the 1st Court of Joint District Judge, Khulna is neither rejected as being nor maintainable. The defendant opposite parties has the opportunity to prefer an appeal as per provision of law.

End.
