full_judgment:
Md Muzammel Hossain J: This petition for leave to appeal under Article 103 of the Constitution of People's Republic of Bangladesh is directed against the judgment and order dated 9-8-2009 passed by a Single Bench of the High Court Division in Civil Revision No. 2278 of 2001 discharging the Rule and affirming the judgment and decree dated 31-1-2001 passed by the learned. Additional District Judge, 3rd Court, Dhaka in Title Appeal No. 214 of 1996 dismissing the appeal and affirming the judgment and decree dated 31-7-1996 passed by the learned Senior Assistant Judge, 6th Court, Dhaka in Title Suit No. 137 of 1996 decreeing the suit for permanent injunction.

2. The present respondent Nos. 1-6 as plaintiffs instituted the Title Suit No. 132 of 1990 before the Court of Assistant Judge, 2nd Court, Dhaka for permanent injunction in respect of 0.17-3/4 acres of land appertaining to CS and. SA Plot No. 367 under CS Khatian No. 136 corresponding to SA Khatian No. 211 and Mutation Khatian No. 211/4 of Mouja Barua. The suit on transfer to the Court of Additional Assistant Judge, 4th Court, Dhaka was renumbered as Title Suit No. 98 of, 1992 which was again transferred to the Court of Assistant Judge, 6th Court, Dhaka and renumbered as Title Suit No. 137 of 1996.

3. The respondent Nos.1-6 as plaintiffs filed the aforesaid suit stating, inter alia, that Omar Ali Sarker was the original owner of the suit land and out of the suit land Abbas Ali Sarker, the son of said Omar Ali Sarker, was the owner and possessor of 7 annas share and Sadar Bewa, wife of Omar Ali, was owner to the extent of 2 arenas share and their names were correctly recorded in the CS Khatian; that Sadar Bewa died leaving one son named Abbas Ali and he became owner of 2 annas share of his mother and in this way, the said Abbas Ali became the owner of 9 annas share in the suit plots and since then he has been possessing the same for more than 12 years; that the said Abbas Ali died leaving behind 2 sons, namely, Asar Ali and Ayub Ali and one wife, Asia Khatun and subsequently said Asia died leaving behind aforesaid 2 sons and they got the land on the basis of amicable partition between the 2 brothers; that when Asgar Ali was in possession and enjoyment of his share in the suit land by cultivating the same and on payment of rent thereof, he transferred 0.16 acres of land out of the land described in schedule of the plaint to Abdus Sattar, predecessor of the plaintiff by a registered deed of sale dated 21-1-1948 and handed over possession to him and thereafter the plaintiff Nos.1 and 6 purchased 0.01-3/4 acres of land from Ayub Ali by a registered deed dated 30-1-1985 and got possession therein; that while father of the plaintiff was in possession and enjoyment of 0.06 acres of land by cultivating various crops thereon, SA and DP Khatians were prepared in his name and thereafter he died leaving behind 2 sons (plaintiff Nos. 2 and 30) and 3 daughters (plaintiff Nos. 1, 4 and 5) and they are in possession and enjoyment of the said land on payment of rent, taxes and mutating their names; that though the defendants have got no right, title, interest and possession in the suit land but on 27-5-1989 the defendants came to take away the crops forcibly but due to intervention they could not succeed in doing the same and in pursuance to that activities of the defendants, the plaintiff No. 1 made GD entry No. 1410 dated 27-5-1989 with the local police station and on investigation the local police found the plaintiff in possession of the suit land; that recently the defendants at the strength of an ineffective deed tried to dispossess the plaintiff forcibly from the suit land but due to timely intervention of the plaintiff and their relatives they could not succeed in doing so but threatened to dispossess them, so the suit.

4. The present petitioner as defendant No. 2 contested the suit by filing the joint written statement denying all the material allegations made in the plaint stating, inter alia, that Omar Ali was the original owner and possessor of the suit land and before CS operation said Omar Ali died leaving behind one wife, Sadar Bewa, 2 sons, named Abbas Ali and Meher Ali and 3 daughters, named Arjan, Samiron and Kadbanu and they inherited the said land according to their shares; that Meher Ali died before CS operation leaving behind only one son Dukkhu Miah; that since the aforesaid 3 daughters were living in the home of their respective husbands CS Khatian has been prepared in the name of Abbas Ali, Dukhu Mia, son of Meher Ali and Sadar Bewa and since then said Dukhu has been enjoying and possessing 0.16 acre of land to the North Eastern side of the suit plot and 0.23 acre to the Southern side and Abbas was in possession and enjoyment of 0.23 of land in the middle of the suit plot on amicable partition and thereafter said Sadar Bewa died leaving Abbas Ali and 3 daughters; that while said Abbas Ali was in possession and enjoyment of the said land, he died leaving one wife, Asia Khatun and 2 sons named Ayub Ali and Asgar Ali and 3 daughters named, Rosia, Monowara and Mukta and on amicable partition Asgar Ali got half from the Western side and half from the Western side and Ayub Ali got half from the Eastern side; that after the death of Abbas Ali his two sons namely, Asgar Ali and Ayub Ali inherited their share from the land left by his father and thereafter Asgar Ali transferred 0.16 acre of land out of said 0.23 acre of land to Abdus Sattar (predecessor of the plaintiff Nos.1-5) by a registered deed of sale dated 21-1-1948 on condition to recovery the same and accordingly on the same date i.e. on 21-1-1948 said Asgar Ali executed and registered a sale deed in favour of Abdus Sattar Raj but Asgar Ali did not handover the said land to Abdus Sattar Raj who had never enjoyed the said land; that 3 months after on 21-1-1948 Asgar Ali returned the said consideration money to Abdus Sattar in presence of Kelajuddin, Belal Uddin, Shahaj Uddin and others and told him to execute and register a deed in favour of him but he did not do so; that subsequently said Asgar Ali transferred the said land to defendant No. 1 by registered deed of sale dated 2-10-1948 and handed over possession to him and since then he has been possessing his own purchased land; that while he was in possession and enjoyment of the said land he transferred 0.0165 acres of land to the plaintiff Nos. 1 and 6 by a registered deed of sale dated 30-1-1985 and handed over possession to them; that the plaintiff Nos. 1 and 5 had never enjoyed and possessed the suit land rather since 2-10-1948 the defendant No. 1 has been possessing the suit land by cultivating various crops; that in the year 1988 the plaintiffs forcibly destroyed the crops cultivated by the defendant in their land and after the said occurrence the defendants filed a petition of complaint being No. 289A 1 of 1988 before the Court of Chief Metropolitan Magistrate and in the said case the learned Magistrate by his judgment and order dated 25-5-1989 convicted the plaintiffs and the learned Magistrate also found the defendants are in exclusive possession in the suit land and on the other hand, the plaintiffs have got no right and possession in the suit land and, as such, the suit of the plaintiffs is not maintainable in its present form, therefore, the same is liable to be dismissed with cost.

5. The learned Senior Assistant Judge, 6th Court, Dhaka by the judgment and decree dated 31-7-1996 decreed the suit. Being aggrieved by the aforesaid judgment and decree the defendant-petitioner preferred Title Appeal No. 214 of 1996 in the Court of District Judge and the learned Additional District Judge, 3 Court, Dhaka by the judgment and decree dated 31-1-2001 dismissed the appeal. Being aggrieved by the aforesaid judgment and decree dated 31-1-2001 the defendant-petitioner moved the High Court Division in Civil Revision No. 2278 of 2001 and a Single Bench of the High Court Division by the impugned judgment and order dated 9-8-2009 discharged the Rule affirming those passed by the court of appeal below.

6. The defendant-petitioner being aggrieved by the impugned judgment and order passed by the High Court Division preferred the instant Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal before this Court.

7. Mr Mahbubey Alam, the learned Advocate for the petitioner submits that since the area of the suit land measuring 17 3/4 decimals out of total land of 62 decimals as described in the schedule of the plaint is not sufficiently identifiable and does not conform to the provision of Order VII Rule 3 of the Code of Civil Procedure, the courts below erred in law in decreeing the suit for permanent injunction and the learned Single Judge of the High Court Division also erred in law in not interfering with the judgment and decree passed by the courts below and, as such, the impugned judgment and order passed by the High Court Division is liable to be set-aside. Mr Alam then submits that the deposition of PWs contradicted each other but the High Court Division committed error of law in affirming the judgment and decree passed by the Court of Appeal below and, as such, the judgment and degree passed by the High Court Division merits interference by this Court. He then submits that though DWs 2 and 3 in their evidence stated that Majida Begum and others or their predecessor Abdus Sattar were never in possession of the suit land the learned Single Judge of the High Court Division without considering the material evidence on record wrongly found that the plaintiffs were in exclusive possession of the suit land and thereby arrived at an erroneous decision calling interference by this Court. He finally submits that since the first deed dated 21-1-1948 followed by the subsequent agreement marked as Exhibit-Ka was not acted upon and was not followed by delivery of possession of 16 decimals of land of the deed and by the second deed dated 30-1-1985 containing 1 3/4 decimals of land the plaintiff Nos. 1 and 6 made a clever man oeuvre to make out a case of exclusive continuous possession of 17 3/4 decimals of land which evidently proved that the plaintiff did not come in the Court with clean hands but the Courts below without considering the points of law decreed the suit and the High Court Division also failed to apply judicial mind in passing the impugned judgment and order which requires interference by this Court.

<u>8. We have heard the learned Advocate appearing for the petitioner, perused the leave petition, impugned judgment and order passed by the High Court Division and all other connected papers on record. It appears that the plaintiff examined 4 witnesses namely, PW Most. Mozida Khatun, PW 2 Yousuf Mollah, PW 3-Suijat Ali and PW 4 Mozuruddin Mollah who adduced evidence in support of the plaintiffs case. They proved plaintiffs exclusive possession in the suit land and they also corroborated each other in support of the plaintiffs case. The defendants by examining the plaintiffs witnesses could not find out any discrepancy as to the possession of the plaintiffs in the suit land. It also appears that there was a criminal case in between the plaintiffs and the defendants and the trial court rightly found that on the basis of judgment passed in criminal case it cannot be said that the defendants are in possession of the suit land. DW 2 Mohsin Sarker in cross-examination stated that the land was not returned by registered deed and there was no written document for payment of Taka 100 in respect of Ekramnama deed. DW 2 Asgar Ali Raj in cross-examination admitted that the land was not returned by registered deed and these witnesses could not say when Sattar Raj was given Taka 100. The High Court Division noticed that both the courts below held that the plaintiffs having deed of 30 years old in respect of suit property cannot be denied their title over the suit land. It also appears that the trial court in cross-examination of DW 2 found that the plaintiffs planted "puishak" (পুইশাক) in the suit land. DW 3 Abdul Awal in cross-examination by the plaintiffs stated there was a suit because the plaintiffs planted "puishak" (পুইশাক) in the suit land. DWA Rahmat Ali Mollah in cross-examination stated that he did not know the exact share of Asgar Ali as he had not seen Asgar Ali. On the other hand, Asgar Ali in cross-examination stated that he left the village 20/25 years ago to East Kamsair. Both the courts below made concurrent findings of facts as to the possession of the plaintiffs in the suit land and that the record of the suit land stands in the name of the plaintiffs and they also got their name mutated and accordingly the suit was decreed by the trial court in favour of the plaintiffs. The court of appeal below also found that the plaintiffs proved their title in the suit land by its registered deed dated 21-1-1948 marked as Exhibit-2. It is well established that in a case for permanent injunction question of title is not material but the possession of parties is material. In the case of Manindra Nath Sen Sarma vs Bangladesh reported in 4 BLD (AD) 285 this Division held that failure to prove title by the plaintiff in a suit for permanent injunction cannot, dis-entitle him to a decree for permanent injunction if he can prove his possession.</u>

<u>9. It appears that the trial court and the court of appeal below made concurrent finding of facts as to the possession of the plaintiffs in the suit land. Both the courts below on consideration of the material evidence on record found that the plaintiffs were able to prove their exclusive possession in the suit land. The High Court Division having considered the evidence of the witnesses rightly found that the Courts below made concurrent findings of fact and there is no misreading or non-consideration of any material evidence on record and the High. Court Division rightly discharged the Rule. In view of the above findings and observations we do not find any merit in the leave petition.</u>

Accordingly, the leave petition is dismissed.

End.

full_judgment:
This Rule, at the instance of defendant-respondent-petitioner, calls in question the legality and propriety of judgment and decree dated 25-4-1995 passed by learned Subordinate Judge, Artha Rin Adalat, Noakhali allowing Title Appeal No. 152 of 1992 and reversing those of dated 13-5-1992 passed by learned Senior Assistant Judge, Begumgonj, Noakhali, dismissing Title Suit No. 14 of 1978.

2. Short facts leading to this Rule are that on 20-1-1978, predecessor of opposite party Nos. 1-7 as plaintiffs instituted Title Suit No. 14 of 1978 in the third Court of Munsif, Sadar, impleading the petitioner and opposite party Nos. 8-29 as defendants for declaration of title in respect of 2.02½ acres of land out of 6.66 acres described in schedule of plaint.

3. Plaintiff's case put in a nutshell are that Wasek Patwari was the owner of suit land in howla interest. Accordingly District Settlement Khatian No. 31 was correctly prepared and published in the name of Wasek Patwari. He died leaving behind four sons namely Asadullah, Chand Mia, Abid Mia and Wakkas Mia, wife Asad Banu, seven daughters namely Maherunnessa, Nesa Bani, Atar Banu, Golap Jan, Tafura Banu, Jahura Khatun, Tafurunnessa as his heirs. Nesa Banu and Tafura Banu sold their share to Aminullah and others. Amin Mia and others sold the said land to Wakkas and Abid Mia, Abid Mia sold his purchased land to Wakkas Mia on 18-1-1927. Wakkas Mia while owing and possessing his inherited and purchased land gifted the same to his daughter on 4-3-1962. The suit land was sold among the co-sharers of plaintiffs and in that process plaintiffs are now owner of 2.02½ acres land. The settlement of the suit land taken by predecessor of the plaintiffs by way of howla interest has been converted into raiyati interest by existing law. The suit land fell in their saham in partition suit No. 53 of 1951 of the Court of Subordinate Judge. During SA operation the same was recorded in the name of predecessor of plaintiffs. They opened holding No. 22 with Tahsil Office and had been paying rent up to 1370 BS. The employees of, defendant No. 1 are not accepting rent from plaintiffs on the plea that Tauzi No. 8 of Superior landlord was sold in auction, which clouded their title Hence the suit.

4. Defendant No.1 (Government) contested the suit by filing written statement denying all material allegations made in plaint contending inter alia that suit land is owned and possessed by government. The suit land along with other land appertaining to District Settlement Khatian No. 31 of Mouza."114 of Bara Newazpur, Upazila Begumganj included in Tauzi No. 8. The said land was sold in auction in Revenue Sale Case No. 114 of 1949-50 and government purchased the land in auction and went into possession. Afterward defendant Nos. 2-4 and others took settlement some of lands from Government on payment of salami and rent and possessing the same SA khatian was not prepared in the name of predecessor of plaintiffs. The howla interest of Wasek Patwari was annulled soon after the auction and notice annulling encumbrance was served upon the heirs of Wasek Patwari. The plaintiffs also applied for taking settlement of some of lands from the Government admitting the auction, plaintiffs filed the suit with evil motive. Therefore, suit is liable to be dismissed.

5. Added defendant Nos. 2-4 also contested the suit by filing written statement stating that government became the owner of suit land pursuant of revenue sale. The government settled the suit land to different persons these defendants though successive heirs of Wasek Patwari took settlement of a portion of suit land by executing Kabuliyat and have Possessed the same. Therefore, suit is also liable to be dismissed:

6. On the pleadings, different issues were settled including the issue of maintainability and the plaintiffs have title and possession in suit land.

7. The trial Court after hearing by judgment and decree dated 22-9-1982 decreed the suit. The decree was reversed in Title Appeal No. 183 of 1982 and suit, was remanded to trial Court for deciding whether title of plaintiffs in respect of suit land was extinguished by auction sale after framing an issue.

8. Then, after hearing, trial Court by judgment and decree dated 13-5-1992 dismissed the suit. On appeal the decree was reversed by Court of appeal below Hence the Rule.

9. The learned Advocate appearing for petitioner submits that predecessor of plaintiffs had no subsisting right, title and interest in suit land inasmuch after admitting auction they took settlement of suit land like the others. Therefore, trial Court rightly dismissed the suit.

<u>10. The learned Counsel appearing for opposite Party Nos. 1-5 and 7 opposes the Rule and submits that Trial Court absolutely misconstrued the notice of Tahsilder dated 12-11-1970 (Exhibit-D) and failed to consider that schedule of land shown in notice, and property claimed by government are not identical. He adds that auction purchased by government was not acted upon and plaintiffs by corroborative evidence succeed to prove their possession. He submits that plaintiffs are paying rents which are evidence of possession. In support of his contentions he refers the case of Erfan Ali vs Joynal Abedin Mia reported in 35 DLR (AD) 216 held:—</u>

<u>"Rent-receipts' are evidence of possession, and may be used as collateral evidence of title.</u>

<u>The rent-receipts were excluded from consideration by the lower Appellate Court taking the view that these are provisional receipts and that they carry little weight in that "any person interested in a land may pay rent to the Government Acquired Estate" This view is erroneous, for rent receipts, though not documents of title, are important items of evidence of possession and may be used as collateral evidence of title since possession generally follows title."</u>

<u>11. The learned counsel further submits that right of howla will not automatically annulled without challenging the same by suit. In support of his contentions he refers the case of Eshaque Ali vs Aitunessa reported in 36 DLR 127 held:—</u>

<u>"Nim-Howla (an encumbrance) does not dis-appear automatically on the sale of the superior interest but has to be annulled by instituting a suit or by other means.</u>

<u>The only question that arises now for our consideration is that whether the Nim-Howla interest of the plaintiffs was annulled by the Government. The Nim-Howla interest of the plaintiff is an encumbrance which is not, ipso-facto, annulled by the revenue sale, but it is annullable at the option of the purchaser. The purchaser may annul under-tenure by institution of a suit or by any other suitable means."</u>

12. The learned counsel lastly submits that defendant No. 1 failed to prove by evidence regarding their possession by way of auction purchase.

<u>13. The learned Assistant Attorney General appearing for opposite party No. 8 also support the Rule and submits that petitioner is the lease under government. He adds that the suit without challenging auction is not maintainable and the same is also barred by limitation. He adds that admitting auction plaintiffs prayed for settlement of suit land. Moreover, plaintiffs failed to prove their own title by evidence. In support of his contentions he refers the case of Md Naimuddin Sardar vs MA Kalam Biswas reported in 39 DLR (AD) 237 held:—</u>

<u>"Plaintiff in order to succeed must establish his own case of obtain a decree and weakness of defendant's case is not ground of passing a decree in favour of the plaintiff"</u>

14. The learned Advocate appearing for opposite party Nos. 9, 14, 21 and 25 supports the Rule and adopted the submissions advanced by learned Assistant Attorney General.

15. In order to appreciate their submissions I have gone through the records and given my anxious consideration to their submissions.

16. The point for consideration whether impugned judgment and decree calls for interference by this Court.

17. Ongoing to materials on record it tan spires that suit land was belonged to Wasek Patwari. Plaintiffs claim that they purchased the land from successive heirs of Wasek Patwari and thereby exercising their right title and possession in suit land. The contesting defendants disowned such facts. They claim that suit land was auctioned in 1949-50 which was purchased by government, therefore howla right of original landlord Wasek Patwari was annulled, and plaintiffs by admitting auction approached for settlement of Government.

18. In course of trial plaintiffs examined three witnesses, of them PW 1 Habibullah husband of original plaintiff Ohedunnessa, he merely stated regarding acquire of land from the Wasek Patwari and they are in possession. PW 2 Saidul Hoq and PW 3 Afzal Mia were examined to corroborate the evidence of PW 1. But on appraisal of their evidence it transpires that PW 1 himself admitted in cross examination that on 21-1-1976 he prayed for settlement of suit land and admitted his signature but his prayer for settlement was rejected. He also failed to state categorically the identify of suit land. Moreover, evidence regarding title and possession in the suit land of the plaintiffs are not Uniform and consistent so the same are vulnerable to the credibility.

19. Moreover, on scrutiny of notice of auction exhibit-A, notice by Tahsilder exhibit-D, basis of title of plaintiffs (Exhibits 3 and 3 ka), it appears that same are identical. Admitting the auction purchase of suit land the plaintiffs approached for settlement of suit land in Misc Case No. 27 of 1976-77.

<u>20. It is pertinent to mention that plaintiffs by way of amendment incorporated the facts regarding auction purchase by Government, although plaintiffs made an unsuccessful attempt to deny such facts and deposed beyond pleadings which disproved their own case.</u>

<u>21. Moreso, plaintiff's title was clouded before institution of instant suit. So, in my view without seeking any relief against auction, the suit for declaration of title simpliciter is not at all maintainable.</u>

22. It appears that all the issues involved in suit have rightly been framed, considered and decided by trial Court with reference to evidence and materials on record but the impugned judgment and decree of the Court of appeal below is not a proper judgment of reversal as it failed to consider the evidence orally and documentary on record and, as such, the Court of appeal below committed an error of law resulting in an erroneous decision occasioning failure of justice.

23. Moreover, the impugned judgment and decree of the Court of appeal below in its entirety are not well founded in the facts and circumstances of the case. So the grounds urged and contentions advanced by the learned Counsel for petitioner are the correct exposition of law and facts and, as such, the legal pleas taken by him prevails and appears to have a good deal of force. On the contrary failed to discover any merit in the submissions advanced by learned Counsel for opposite party Nos. 1-5 and 7. However I have gone through the decisions reported in 35 DLR (AD) 216 and 36 DLR 127 as referred by him. I am in respectful agreement with the principles enunciated therein but facts leading to those cases are distinguishable to that of the instant case, therefore I am also unable to accept him sub-missions.

24. Having considered the facts and circumstances of the case and foregoing narrative, I am of the view that the impugned judgment and decree suffers from legal infirmities, which calls for interference by this Court. Thus the Rule having merit succeeds.

25. In the result, the Rule is made absolute without any order as to cost. The impugned judgment and decree dated 25-4-1995 passed in Title Appeal No. 152 of 1992 is hereby set aside, consequently Title Suit No. 14 of 1978 is dismissed.

Office is directed to send down the records of the case at once.

End.

full_judgment:
Syed Mahmud Hossain J: This appeal by leave by the appellant is directed against the judgment and order dated 29-10-1998 passed by the High Court Division in Civil Revision No. 502 of 1995 discharging the Rule and affirming the judgment and decree dated 24-9-1994 passed by the learned Subordinate Judge (now Joint District Judge), Third Court, Dhaka dismissing Title Appeal No. 291 of 1989 and affirming the judgment and decree dated 5-9-1989 passed by the learned Assistant Judge, First Court, Dhaka in Title Suit No. 329 of 1988 rejecting the plaint under Order VII, rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure.

2. The facts, leading to this appeal, are precised below:

The suit property appertaining to Plot No. 4166 of SA Khatian No.1359 of Mouza-Wari, PS Sutrapur, Dhaka, measuring an area of 0.3080 acre with appurtenances originally belonged to Sreemoti Labanga Lata Chowdhury, wife of late Ramdulal Ganguly. On 19-2-1984, the suit property was requisitioned by the Government in Requisition Case Nos.192/48 and 3/4 share of the suit property was allotted to the husband of plaintiff No. 1, late Gowher Jamil and the remaining 1/4 share of the suit property to the father of plaintiff No. 2, late Lokman Hakim, while they were in service under the Government. While residing over the suit property Gowher Jamil, the husband of plaintiff No. 1 erected a semi pucca corrugated iron shed and started an institution in the name and style, Jago Art Centre. Subsequently, the husband of plaintiff No. 1 as a Director of Jago Art Center got allotment of 3/4 share of the suit property from defendant No. 3 in the name of Jago Art Center. Gowher Jamil started the Jago Art Center to impart dancing lessons in dance and to promote the culture of music and dance in the country. On 22-9-1980, Gowher Jamil, the Director of the Jago Art Center, died in a road accident and after his death, plaintiff No. 1 became the Director. On the death of Lokman Hakim, plaintiff No. 2 got allotment of the suitproperty who was also an employee. of the, Government. While in possession of the suit property, they got a notice from defendant No. 2, Additional Deputy Commissioner (ADC) (LA), Dhaka on 30-7-1985 and came to know that the suit property had been de-requisitioned in favour of its owner Harlal Ganguly on 22-2-1948 and the plaintiffs were directed to hand over possession of the suit property. After getting this notice, they became astonished as to how the suit property was de-requisitioned in favour of Harlal Ganguly, who died long before. After that, defendant No. 2, ADC (LA), Dhaka gave reminder to them to hand over possession of the suit property by 31-5-1986 failing which they would be evicted therefrom. But they did not hand over possession of the suit property in favour of defendant No.2, who again served a notice on 7-9-1986 to hand over possession of the suit property by 16-10-1986. Finding no other alternative, they filed Title Suit No. 201 of 1986 in the Court of Assistant Judge, Dhaka on 28-6-1986, challenging the order of de-requisition dated 22-2-1986 and also the notice dated 7-9-1986. The suit was decreed ex parte on 18-4-1987 as the defendants did not file any written statement. Against the ex parte decree dated 18-4-1987, defendant Nos. 2-4 preferred Title Appeal No. 133 of 1987 before the learned District Judge, Dhaka. On transfer, the appeal was heard and disposed of by the learned Additional District Judge, Dhaka who allowed the appeal setting aside the ex parte decree passed by the trial Court and also dismissed the suit on the ground of maintainability under section 14A of the East Bengal (Emergency) Requisition of Property Act, 1948. Harlal Ganguly during those long years did not come to the suit property and he also did not receive the rent of the suit property Defendant No. 1 has created a forged and collusive document in respect of the suit property on 1-6-1983 in the name of Harlal Ganguly and on the basis of this collusive document, he has been trying to mutate his name. Defendant No. 1 in collusion with defendant No. 2 managed to get the order of de-requisition of the suit property in favour of Harlal Ganguly on 22-2-1984. The order of de-requisition dated 22-2-1984 is collusive and illegal. Defendant Nos. 2-4 in collusion with defendant No. 1 have been trying to evict the plaintiffs from the suit property. The deed of sale dated 1-6-1983 in favour of defendant No. 1 by. Harlal Ganguly is collusive and forged and, as such, on the basis of this deed, he cannot get possession of the suit property. After that, defendant Nos. 2-4 in collusion with defendant No. 1 has been threatening the plaintiffs to dispossess them from the suit property on the basis of his forged and collusive deed dated 1-6-1983. Hence this suit has been filed.

3. Defendant Nos. 1-4 contested the case by filing two separate applications under Order VII, Rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure for rejecting the plaint as being barred by law. After filing of these applications for rejection of the plaint, the learned Assistant Judge fixed the date of hearing and after hearing both sides passed a judgment on 5-9-1989 rejecting the plaint.

4. Against the judgment and decree dated 5-9-1989 passed by the learned Assistant Judge, the plaintiffs preferred Title Appeal No. 291 of 1989 before the learned District Judge, Dhaka. On transfer, the appeal was heard by the then learned Subordinate Judge, Third Court, Dhaka, who by his judgment and order dated 24-9-1994 dismissed the appeal affirming the judgment and decree of the learned Assistant Judge.

5. Being aggrieved by and dissatisfied with the judgment and decree dated 24-9-1994, plaintiff No.1 filed a revisional application before the High Court Division and obtained Rule in Civil Revision No. 502 of 1995. The High Court Division by the judgment and order dated 29-10-1998 discharged the Rule on contest against respondent No. 1 and ex parte against the rest without any order as to costs.

6. Feeling aggrieved by and dissatisfied with judgment and order passed by the High Court Division, plaintiff No. 1 as the leave-petitioner moved this Division by filing Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No. 297 of 1999, in which, leave was granted on 24-10-2000 resulting in the initiation of Civil Appeal No. 223 of 2000. During pendency of the appeal, the sole appellant died and she was substituted by her daughter.

7. Mr Khijir Ahmed, learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the appellant, submits that the High Court Division erroneously came to a finding that the case is barred under section 42 of the Specific Relief Act and that the plaint is liable to be rejected under Order VII Rule 11(d) of the Code of Civil Procedure and, as such, the impugned judgment should be set-aside. He further submits that the findings of the High Court Division that the suit is barred under section 14A of the (Emergency) Requisition of Property Act, 1948 is erroneous and, as such, the impugned judgment is liable to be set-aside.

8. Mr Abdul Wadud Bhuiyan, learned Senior Advocate appearing on behalf of respondent No. 1, on the other hand, submits that the plaintiffs did not have any legal character in respect of the suit property and, as such, the plaint can be rejected by resorting to the provision of section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure. In support of his submissions, he relied upon two cases of this Division, which we shall discuss in the body of the judgment.

9. We have considered the submissions of the learned Advocates, perused the impugned judgment and the materials on record.

10. Before addressing the submissions made by the learned Advocate for the appellant, it is necessary to go through the submissions of the learned Advocate, on which, leave was granted as under:

"While rejecting a plaint under Order VII, Rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure, the Court is only to look into the averment made in the plaint and nothing else. But here in the present case while passing the order of rejection of the plaint the trial Court, appellate Court as well as the High Court Division lost sight of the legal position and entered into the defence version of the case. The High Court Division also committed illegality in holding that the suit is barred by res judicata though as a matter of fact without taking the evidence this cannot be decided. The application under section 14A of the Acquisition and Requisition of Immovable Property Ordinance,1948 is uncalled for and is illegal and while deciding the matter, the Courts below over looked the clear provision of section VII Rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure and its jurisdiction and the application."

11. Admittedly, the suit property was requisitioned by the Government on 19-2-1949 in Requisition Case No. 148 of 1948. The suit property was allotted to Gowher Jamil and Lokman Hakim, father of respondent No. 5, while they were in service of the Government. On their death, allotment was given to the appellant Mrs Rawshan Jamil (since deceased) and respondent No.5 who had been in possession of the suit property Late Gowher Jamil, husband of Mrs Rawshan Jamil (since deceased) started an institution in the suit land under the name and style, Jago Art Centre, to impart lessons in dance and to promote the culture of music and dance in the country. The suit property, which was requisitioned by the Government from Harlal Ganguly was subsequently de-requisitioned on 22-2-1984. Soon after passing of the order of derequisition in favour of Harlal Ganguly, Mrs Rawshan Jamil, the appellant (since deceased) and respondent No. 5 were asked to vacate the suit property. Mrs Rawshan Jamil and respondent No. 5 as the plaintiffs instituted Title Suit No. 201 of 1986 in the Sixth Court of the learned Assistant Judge for declaration of title that the order of de-requisition and the notice issued upon them for vacating the suit property were illegal, without jurisdiction and not binding upon them. That suit was decreed ex parte against respondent No. 1 and others, who preferred Title Appeal No. 133 of 1986. The appeal was allowed and the ex parte decree was set-aside and the suit was found to be barred by law. After that, Mrs Rawshan Jamil and respondent No. 5 as the plaintiffs filed Title Suit No. 329 of 1988 in the Court of Assistant Judge, First Court, Dhaka for declaration that the deed of sale dated 1-6-1983 alleged to have been executed by Harlal Ganguly in favour of respondent No.1 in respect of the suit property was forged, collusive and void.

12. The learned Assistant Judge rejected the plaint of Title Suit No. 329 of 1988. Against the judgment and decree of the learned Assistant Judge, the plaintiffs filed Title Appeal No. 294 of 1989 before the learned District Judge, Dhaka. The then learned Subordinate Judge, who heard the appeal affirmed the judgment and decree of the learned Assistant Judge by his judgment and decree dated 14-9-1994.

13. Against the judgment and decree passed by the appellate Court, Mrs Rawshan Jamil filed a revisional application before the High Court Division in which Rule was issued in Civil Revision No. 502 of 1995. After hearing the parties, the High Court Division discharged the Rule by the impugned judgment dated 29-10-1998.

14. In order to resolve the issues involved in this appeal, it is necessary to go through the prayer portion of the plaint of Title Suit No. 329 of 1988, which is quoted below:

“(ক) কিশোরগঞ্জ জিলাধীন কিশোরগজ্ঞ সদর সুদাকিয়া নিবাসী মৃত রাম দুলাল গাংগুলির পুত্র কথিত বাবু হরলাল গাংগুলি কিশোরগজ্ঞ সদর আখারা বাজার নিবাসী মৃত হাজী আখতার উদ্দিন আহম্মদের পুত্র মোঃ আদিলজ্জামান বরাবরে নালিশী সম্পত্তির বিগত ১-৮-১৯৮৩ ইং তারিখে সম্পাদিত এবং উক্ত একই তারিখে ঢাকার তেজগাঁও সাব-রেজিষ্ট্রারীকৃত সাফ কবলা দলিল যাহার বুক নং ১, ভলিউম নং ৪৯ পৃষঠা নং ১১, ৭, ১১২, দলিল নং ৩০৪৩ বৎসর  ১৯৮০ তাহা ভূয়া জাল বানোয়াট পন বিহীন ভাক্ত অবৈধ যোগ সাজসী শঠতা পূর্বক এবং অকার্য্যকর এই মর্মে এক ঘোষণামূলক ডিক্রি দিতে আঙ্গা হয়।

(খ) মোকদ্দমার সমস্ত খরচের ডিক্রি দিতে আজ্ঞা হয় ।

(গ) অন্যান্য প্রতিকার যাহা বাদীগণ আইনতঃ এবং ন্যায়ত পাইতে হকদার তাহার ও ডিক্রি দিতে আজ্ঞা হয়।”

15. The High Court Division came to a finding that the plaintiffs as allottees could not claim to have their legal right and character in bringing the suit over the requisitioned property in which they had no right and that in that consideration the learned Subordinate Judge held that the suit was barred under section 42 of the Specific Relief Act.

<u>16. If the plaintiffs do not have any legal character/interest in the suit property, in such a situation, the plaint can be rejected by resorting to the provision of section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure and in the instant case, the plaintiffs went into possession on the basis of allotment given by the Government, which requisitioned the disputed property. As soon as the Government de-requisitioned the suit property and issued notice upon the plaintiffs for vacating the suit property, they did not have any legal right to file the suit.</u>

17. In this connection, reliance may be placed on the case of Burmah Eastern Ltd. Vs Burmah Eastern Employees Union (1966) 18 DLR (Dacca) 709, which is as under:

"Turning, now, to the plaint in the present suit, it is obvious, from a mere perusal of the plaint itself, that it must be held that the suit is prohibited under, if not by law. This being the position, even if the case does not come, literally and strictly, within the letter of order VII, rule 11 of the Code of Civil procedure, there cannot be any manner of doubt that the suit is prohibited under the law in the sense that it is barred under legal provisions. The Court below should, therefore, have rejected the plaint in limine because the suit itself is barred under our legal system. If Order VII, rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure cannot be prayed in aid, the inherent power of the Court should be invoked.

18. The principle of law deduced in the above case is that if a perusal of the plaint reveals that the suit is not prohibited under any law then the provision of Order VII, Rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure cannot be invoked. But if the suit is prohibited under the law in the sense that it is barred under legal provisions, the plaint may be rejected by invoking section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure. The plaint of the present suit cannot be rejected by resorting to Order VII, Rule 11 as the suit is not barred by any law. But the plaintiffs did not have any legal interest as required under section 42 of the Specific Relief Act and in such a situation, the plaint can be rejected under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure.

19. In the case of Abdul Jalil vs Islami Bank Bangladesh Limited, (2011) 53 DLR (AD)12, it has been held that it is well settled that where a plaint cannot be rejected under Order VII, Rule 11, the Court may invoke its inherent jurisdiction and reject the plaint taking recourse to section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure.

20. In the case in hand, the plaintiffs do not have any legal interest in the suit property and the interest which they derived from the Government was extinguished as soon as the property was de-requisitioned by the Government, which issued notice upon the plaintiffs to vacate the said premises.

21. Reliance may be placed on the case of Capital Tower Ltd. Vs Mirpur Mazar Co-operative Market Society Ltd. 56 DLR (AD) 8, in which, paragraph-17, it has been held as under:

"17. As to the maintainability of the suit in spite of not being one covered by the provision of section 42 of the Specific Relief Act the learned Counsel for respondent No.1 has referred to the decisions reported ILR 22 Madras 270, AIR 1925 PC 36, AIR 1979 SC 114, (1911) 1 KB 410, (1953) 2 QB 18, AIR 1975 SC 1810, 9 PLR (Dhaka Series) 477 and 8 BLC (AD) 111. The principle enunciated in the aforesaid cases that outside the scope of section 42 of the Specific Relief Act declaration can be sought for, in our opinion, can hardly be disputed, but the fact remains that the relief so sought for by the plaintiff not is at all available to him while he has no legal interest in the subject matter of the suit."

Though the above case is not on rejection of plaint, the principle expounded in the above case is that the plaintiff cannot get any relief unless he has any legal interest in the subject matter of the suit. In the instant case, admittedly, the plaintiffs did not have any legal interest in the subject matter of the suit and, as such, the plaint is liable to be rejected under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure.

22. The High Court Division wrongly concurred with the findings of the Courts below that the suit is barred by Res Judicata and, as such, the plaint is liable to be rejected under Order VII, Rule 11 of the Code Civil Procedure.

<u>23. What is important to note here is that Order VII, Rule 11 Clause (d) is not available for rejection of a plaint under section 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure. The plea of res judicata as contained in section 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure can be resolved at the trial after framing an issue and cannot be decided from a reading of the plaint. Similar opinions have been expressed in the case of Sreemati Pushpa Rani Das vs AKM Habibur Rahman (1993) 13 BLD (AD) 217 and the case of Abdul Jalil vs Islami Bank Bangladesh Ltd. in Civil Appeal No.204 of 2003 in which judgment was delivered on 12-10-2011.</u>

24. The High Court Division wrongly concurred with the finding of the Courts below that the suit is barred under section 14A of the (Emergency) Requisition and Acquisition of Property Act, 1948. Having gone through the prayer portion of the plaint of Title Suit No.329 of 1988, it appears that the plaintiffs sought no relief against the order of derequisition and they even did not challenge the notices issued upon them to vacate the suit premises. Therefore, Title Suit No.329 of 1988 was not barred under section 14A of the (Emergency) Requisition and Acquisition of Property Act, 1948.

25. All the Courts below erroneously came to a finding that the plaint was liable to be rejected under Clause-(d) of Order VII, rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure. But in the instant case, the plaint should have been rejected under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure in the light of the findings made before and, as such, the plaint shall be deemed to have been rejected under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure.

Therefore, we do not find any valid ground for interference with the impugned judgment. Accordingly, the appeal is dismissed.

End.

The heirs of the original defendants have preferred this revisional application under section 115(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure and upon hearing the learned Advocate this Court issued the Rule on the following terms:

"Let the records of the case be called for an Rule issue calling upon the opposite party .Nos.1-8 to show cause as to why the judgment and order dated 6-2-2005 passed in Miscellaneous Appeal No. 44 of 2004 passed by the learned Additional District Judge, 2nd Court, Gazipur dismissing the appeal and affirming the judgment and order No. 84 dated 25-4-2004 passed in Miscellaneous Case No. 16 of 2002 by the learned Joint District Judge 1st Court, Gazipur should not be set aside and/or pass such other order, or further order or orders as to this Court may seem fit and proper."

2. Facts relevant for disposal of the Rule are that the plaintiffs instituted partition suit No. 166 of 1979 on' 29-3-1979 in the Court of Subordinate Judge, Dhaka, subsequently the suit was transferred to Subordinate Judge, Gazipur and renumbered as partition suit No. 1317 of 1985 and the aforesaid suit was decreed ex-parte on 30-12-1987 and decree was signed on 27-5-1989.

3. Against the said ex-parte judgment and decree dated 30-12-1987 heirs of defendant No. 2 and others filed Miscellaneous Case No. 16 of 2002 under Order IX, rule 13 read with section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure for set-ting aside the ex-parte judgment and decree. The case of the applicants made out in Miscellaneous case in short is that opposite parties as plaintiffs proceeded with Title Suit No. 1317 of 1985 and after transfer ultimately, the suit was disposed of ex-parte, by judgment and decree dated 30-11-1987 and against the aforesaid judgment and decree, the petitioners filed above mentioned Miscellaneous Case under Order IX, rule 13read with section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure for setting aside the judgment and decree stating inter alia that the judgment and decree were obtained by practicing fraud upon the Court. The summons were not served upon the defendants and at the time of institution of the suit some of the defendants were dead. The plaintiffs fraudulently shown those summons were served upon the defendants. On 25-4-2005 few people assembled in the suit land and seeing the assembly of people, inquired out of curiosity about their presence who then disclosed that they have come to execute the decree passed by Subordinate Judge, 1st Court, Gazipur and hearing about such decree Habibur Rahman raised objection verbally and on such protest the process server could not deliver the possession and thereafter, said Habibur Rahman on 27-4-2002 got searched the record and came to known that Mahabat Ullah Sarker son of Harmat Ullah Sarker instituted the suit and got the ex-parte preliminary decree on 30-12-1987 and decree was signed on 8-1-2002 but no summons or notice were served. on the petitioners and obtained the and suppressing the facts fraudulently and stated further that before the filing of the suit the defendants died but the heirs of the defendants were not substituted but the plaintiffs obtained the decree against the dead person, and as such decree is a nullity when filed the case.

4. The plaintiff opposite party Nos. 1-8 filed joint written objection and denied the allegations made in the application under Order IX, rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure and stated that the predecessors of the present petitioners were made parties in the partition suit. The summons were duly served upon the defendants but they did not contest the suit. The judgment and decree in question were passed in accordance with law but the petitioners, filed the Miscellaneous case on some false allegations and as such, the Miscellaneous Case is liable to be dismissed with cost and stated further that Advocate Commissioner after the preliminary decree went to the suit land on 5-8-1991 and after measurement of suit land, filed the report on 5-10-1991 and on the basis of the report final decree was passed. It has further been stated that at the time of measurement, the petitioners and local people were present and in spite of that they did not raise and objection and that the story introduced in the application is false and baseless and have filed the Miscellaneous Case of harass the decree holder only.

5. The petitioner examined 2 PWs and plaintiff opposite party examined opposite party No. 1 to prove their respective case.

6. The Joint District Judge upon considering the evidence and records dismissed the Miscellaneous Case by order dated 25-4-2004.

7. Against the aforesaid judgment and order the heirs of the defendants petitioners preferred Appeal before the District Judge, Gazipur. Eventually, the appeal was disposed of by the Additional District Judge, 2nd Court, Gazipur who disallowed the appeal by judgment and order dated 6-2-2005.

8. The petitioner-appellants being aggrieved by the aforesaid judgment and order of the Appellate Court has preferred this revisional application and obtained the Rule as stated above.

9. Mr Faruq Ahmed, the learned Advocate with Ms Anjuman Ara Begum, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the above petitioners has taken me through the judgments and orders passed by the Courts below and also placed the application under Order IX, rule 13 read with section 151 and the written objection filed by the plaintiff-opposite-parties and other materials from the records and submitted that both the Courts had not taken trouble to see the order sheet as to whether the summons/notices were served upon the defendants No.  2, 3, 5, 7 and 8 which is vital for the purpose of the disposal of the case under Order IX, rule 13 which has been filed mainly on the assertion that before holding the trial of the suit by the Subordinate Judge at Gazipur, the aforesaid defendants died and thereby, the judgments and orders suffer from non consideration of the materials as well as Order LXI, but the Courts below held that the summons and the notices were served upon the defendants and  as such, the trial Court as well as the Appellate Court have committed error of law which is an error in the decision occasioning failure of justice.

10. Mr Faruq also placed Annexure A, the report of the process server regarding the service of summons and submitted that it would be evident from the report itself that the summons were not served on defendant Nos. 2, 3 ,5, 7 and 8 in as such as report dated 19-4-1979 says:

ইতি,

১৯-৪-৭৯

and the report indicates the summons were served but allegedly served on defendant Nos. 1, showing defendant No. 1 as ভারপ্রাপ্ত কর্মকর্তা which accordingly to the provision of order 5 rule 17 is not a service and then he has referred the order dated 28-6-1982.

"SR served. (illegible) seen. But not satisfactory; Plaintiff to file postal requisites on defendants No.  2-3, 5 and 7-20 by 16-8-1982."

And order No. 32 dated 1-11-1982.

"Plaintiff files hazira but lawyer not available. However, for the ends of justice to 19-12-1982 for hearing the petition

Order No. 35 dated 16-3-1983.

"Requisites filed. Issue same on amended defendants fixing 2-5-1953 for SR and order plaintiff takes no step as per order of 28-6-1982. Plaintiff to take step by the date fixed,"

and submitted that thereafter, no step taken by the plaintiff to comply with the order of the Court. Mr Faruq referring to the counter affidavit filed by the plaintiff opposite parties herein submits that the Trial Court has stated that the summons on the predecessor of the petitioners No. 1-8 that is the defendant No. 2 Hashmat Ullah served on 10,8-1986 which has been quoted in the paragraph 5 of the counter affidavit and submitted, relying upon his reply that the summons as stated by the learned Subordinate Judge has not been served, as such and he has also shown from the order sheet that no such order was passed on 10-8-1986 but orders were passed on 25-6-1986 and 13-8-1986 and submitted and such findings is based on no materials rather it is a non consideration of the materials and such findings arrived at on conjectures and as such, the judgments and orders suffer from material irregularities for which the same are liable to be set aside.

11. The learned Advocate for the petitioners further submits that the onus lies on the plaintiff to prove the service of summons upon the defendants but the plaintiffs did not examine the process server to prove the service of summons and also did not produce any wit-nesses to corroborate the evidence of OPW produced on behalf of the plaintiff opposite parties but the Courts below were quite oblivious on this vital aspect of the case and on the face of such materials on record rejecting the application under Order IX, rule 13, both the Courts have committed error of law resulting an error in the decision occasioning failure of justice.

12. To support of his contention several cases have been cited before this Court such as (i) in the case of Santosh Kumar Chakraborty vs MA Motaleb Hossain reported in 1985 BLD (AD) 59 = 36 DLR (AD) 248 , their Lordships held in paragraph 6:

"Khondkar Mahbubuddin Ahmed, learned Advocate for the respondents while defending the High Court Division's judgment contended that the very proceedings under Order IX, rule 13 CPC became in fructuous as the ex-parte decree was fully satisfied through execution, that the necessary sale-deed was executed and registered by the Court and possession of the land was also delivered as there was no order from the superior Court staying the Execution proceeding. Mr Rafique-ul-Huq how-ever contends that the execution of an ex parte decree does not render the application for setting aside the ex parte decree in fructuous, for, even after execution of the decree the petitioner has got remedy by way of restitution under section 144 CPC; and in support of this contention, the learned Advocate has referred to a number of decision, particularly the decision in the case of Keshab Chandra vs Baliganj Estate Pvt. Limited 76 CWN 281. We find substance in this contention and hold that the proceedings under Order IX, rule 13 did not become in fructuous by the earlier execution of the decree".

(ii) in the case of Abdur Rashid vs Abdul Barik reported in 35 DLR (AD) 162 their Lord-ships observe paragraph 10:

"Under Order IX, rule 13 of the Code of summons is not duly served on the defendant, that is a good ground for setting aside an ex-parte decree. On a perusal of the relevant provisions of the Civil Procedure Code it would be apparent, that due service of summons is an essential condition which must be satisfied before the Court can proceed to give a judgment and under Order IX, rule 13 if a party satisfies the Court that summons were not duly service upon him, the Court is bound to set aside the ex-parte decree. In such a case question of knowledge is not at all relevant and ex-parte decree will be set aside even if the defendant had knowledge of institution of a suit. No provision of the law could be pointed out by the learned Council for the respondent, which dispenses with the necessity of proper service of summons".

(iii) In the case of Upendra Chandra Rishi vs Sufia Begum reported in 1990 BLD (AD) 194 = 42 DLR (AD) 285 their Lordships held in paragraphs 17, 18 and 19:

"17. Since this is allegedly a case of refusal to accept service the following provisions of Order V, rule 17 of the Code of Civil Procedure are to be kept in view:

"17. Where the defendant or his age or such other person as aforesaid refusal to sign the acknowledgement, or where the serving officer, after using all due and reasonable diligence cannot find the defendant and there is no agent empowered to accept service of the summons on his behalf, of any other person on whom service can be made, the serving officer shall affix a copy of the summons on the outer door or some other conspicuous part of the house in which the defendant ordinarily resides of carries on business or personally works for gain, and shall then return the original to the Court from which it was issued; with a report endorsed thereon or annexed there stating that he has so affixed they copy the circumstances under which he did so, and the name and address of the person (if any) by whom the house was identified and it whose presence the copy was affixed."

"18. It is, therefore obligatory upon the process server to mention in this report the name and address of the person, if any, by whom the house was identified and in whose presence the copy was affixed. "

Also relevant is Rule 84(e) of the Civil Rules and Orders which provides as follows:

"(e) where a person refuses to accept the process the grounds thereof, if any, and the names of the persons witnessing the refusal should be given."

"19. The service reports, Ext. A series, are devoid of these essential information. The Courts below and the High Court Division have failed to consider the Order Sheet and the relevant provisions of law."

(iv) In the case of Bangladesh vs Mashiur Rahman reported in 50 DLR (AD) 205 where their lordships observed in paragraph No.

"18. It is a cardinal principle of administration of justice that no result of any judicial proceeding should be allowed to receive judicial approval from any Court of law whenever it is obtained by practicing fraud upon the Court; reason being fraud demolishes the very foundation of sanctity of such judicial proceeding. It is also well established principle of law that fraud vitiates all judicial proceedings. Thus contravention of the provision of law cannot be a valid ground for allowing an order obtained by fraud to stand When the trial Court itself on consideration of the materials on record was satisfied that a fraud had been committed in obtaining the ex-parte decree it was the duty of the trial Court to set aside the ex-parte decree. The failure of the trial Court in the performance of its legal obligations ought not to have been maintained by the High Court Division in affirming the finding of the trial Court."

13. The learned Advocate finally submits that in the case under Order IX, rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure, if the petitioners can substantiate cause for non appearance at the time of hearing of the suit, it can be restored upon cost and submitted further that the heirs of the defendant have been able to prove that the summons and the notices were not served upon them and as such, the petitioner may be allow to contest the suit by setting aside, the ex-parte decree. In support of his contention he refers the case of Abdul Hamid Khan vs Miah Nurul Islam reported in 42 DLR (AD) 48, their Lordships held in paragraph 5:

"5. After considering the facts and circumstances of the case we find that there is some substance in the contentions of the learned counsel for the appellant. We set aside the judgments and orders of the Courts below and allow the Miscellaneous Case No. 28 of 1983. Let Title Suit No. 9 of 1983 of the Second Court of Subordinate Judge, Mymensingh be restored to its file and number. The appellant is, however, to pay a sum of Taka 2,500 towards the respondent's legal expenses within two months from the receipt of notice from the trial Court, failing which the appeal shall stand dismissed."

14. Mr Sk Shamsul Alam the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the plaintiff opposite party Nos.1-8 has candidly refuted the submissions of the learned Advocate for the petitioners and submitted that the trial Court upon consideration of the evidence of the parties and taking note of the evidence has clearly found that the summons/notice were served upon the defendants, the predecessor of the petitioners and having full satisfaction on the service as well as the evidence on record dismissed the application under Order IX, rule 13 finding that the causes for non appearance shown before the Court could not be proved and committed no error of law which calls for no interference by this Court. The learned Advocate also submitted that the Appellate Court having regard to the provision of Order 41, rule 31 has independently considered the evidence of the parties along with other materials and elaborately discussed the evidence and held that the petitioners, the heirs of original defendants could not prove their case that summons were not served upon their predecessor and having been satisfied on the evidence with reference to the service of summons recorded clear findings and disallowed the appeal concurring with the findings and decision of the trial Court and hereby, both the Courts below committed no error of law in exercising their power as provided by law and as such, the judgments and orders do not suffer from any illegalities which calls for interference by the Hon'ble Court in the revisional jurisdiction. He further submits that the Courts below settled the .facts considering the evidence on record and in that case the revisional Court needs not interfere as facts were settled by the Appellate Court being the final Court of facts.

15. In support of his contention several authorities are cited by the learned Advocate such (a) In the case of Md Shah Alam vs Farida Begum reported in 1997 BLD (AD) 145 = 2 BLC (AD) 92, (b) in the case of Amanatullah vs Ali Mohammad Bhuiyan reported in 1997 BLD (AD) 199 = 2 BLC (AD) 134, (c) In the case of Md Shah Jahan vs Mir Hossain reported in 1997 BLD (AD) 218, (d) In the case of Hazari Bala Sana vs Niron alias Niranjan Mandal reported in 1997 BLD (AD) 294.

16. The learned Advocate then refers to order No. 9 dated 16-1-1980 from the Trial Court's order sheet which disclosed "summons served on defendants 1 to 19 SR on defendant No. 20 not served. To 22-2-1980 for SR on defendant No.  20—for order and further submitted that upon further direction of the Court the plaintiffs had put in requisites and those were served on the defendants which is being reflected in order No. 61 dated' 13-9-1986 "Later AD upon the defendant Nos. 4-7, 1(f) 1(m), 11(a), 12, 1(c), 1(h), 1(j) received duly served. AD also received answered on defendant No.  13. To date also for step by the plaintiff" and submitted that the notice were served and upon consideration of the service of summons and notices the Courts below found that the ex-parte decree was passed upon proper consideration of the materials on record and as such, calls for no interference in revisional jurisdiction. The learned Advocate referring to the written objection has submitted further that after the ex-parte decree the Advocate Commissioner visited the schedule land and prepared the report which were witnessed by the present petitioners but did not raise objection at the relevant time and subsequently, came up with the present application under Order IX, rule 13 just to harass he plaintiff opposite parties and those aspect of the case were clearly noticed by the Courts below and being satisfied have dismissed the application under Order IX, rule 13 read with section 151 and hereby committed no error of law and the Courts below being the Appellate Court and being final Court of facts disallowed the appeal affirming the judgment and order of the Trial Court and committed no error of law resulting an error in the decision occasioning failure of justice.

17. Mr Alam has cited several other decisions to substantiate his contention that when ever the facts settled by the Courts below upon concurrent finding that cannot be legally interfered by the revisional Court such as : (a) In the case of Mazharul Borhan vs AH Bhuiyan reported in 1995 BLD (AD) 237, (b) In the case of Haidernessa vs Monowara Begum reported in 1996 BLD (AD) 280 para 6 and 7, (c) In the case Akrab Ali vs Zahiruddin Kari reported in 30 DLR (SC) 81 para 14 and (d) In the case of Jasimuddin Kanchan vs Md Ali Ashraf reported in 42 DLR (AD) 289 para 13B:

"This finding, based on due consideration of evidence, was beyond the scope of the revisional Court to interfere with. Executants of the kabala Exhibit 1 had no title to the land far transfer to the respondent."

18. Mr Alam the learned Advocate, finally urged that the High Court Division does not need to interfere, so long there are other remedy by separate suit and against the self same judgment a partition suit being No. 171 of 2005 and another partition suit No. 233 of 2005 are pending wherein, the present petitioners are contesting the suit, in that view of the matter the petitioners will have opportunity to adduce evidence and contest the suits on merit and as such, the Rule is liable to be discharged.

19. The learned Advocate further submitted that section 107 of the Evidence Act provides the burden of proving that a person in dead, is on the person who affirms it and submitted that the petitioners could not prove the death of the predecessor and to support his contention refers the case of Abul Hashem (Bulbul) vs Mobarak Uddin Mahmud reported in 1986 BLD 250, wherein their Lordships held that a general statement that the person were dead or absent without giving specific evidence to that effect is of no assistance to the petitioner.

20. Mr Faruq Ahmed the learned Advocate, for the petitioners in reply submitted that the petitioner having regard to the provision of law had preferred this revisional application under section 115(1) which has been done legally within the scope of law at the relevant point of time and other sets of defendants challenged the propriety of the decree passed in the partition suit No. 1317 of 1985 and made the present petitioners parties and as of necessity the petitioners appeared in the suit, but that does not preclude the petitioners in getting justice under section 115(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure and the submissions of the learned Advocate for the opposite party do not tenable in law.

<u>21. In view of the submission of the 'learned Advocate, I have examined the order sheet of the Trial Court which has been referred by the learned Advocate and found that the order No.  9 dated 16-1-1980 as quoted above, the process server submitted report to have served the notice and the same is also reflected from the Annexure A, report of the process server but by subsequent order dated 28-6-1982, the Court asked the plaintiffs to put in fresh requisites in respect of defendant Nos. 2, 3, 8 and 7-20 (order No.  30) and by the subsequent order No.  35 dated 16-3-1963, the Court found non compliance of the order and further asked the plaintiff to comply with the order dated 28-6-1982 and from the said order No. 61, it appears that subsequently notices were served on defendant Nos. 4-7 and substituted heirs of defendant Nos. 1(f), 1(m), 1(a), 11(a), 12, 1(c), 1(h), 1(j) but we do not find any order to have passed on 10-8-1986 as referred by the learned Trial Court in his judgment which has been quoted by the learned Advocate for the plaintiff opposite parties in paragraph 5 of the counter affidavits and we also do not find any service of summons upon defendant Nos. 2, 3 and 8 and on the face of such materials on record, I have drawn the attention of the learned Advocate for the plaintiff opposite parties to such facts who finds difficulty to trace any order as to have passed on 10-8-1986 by the Trial Court and also any order as to service of summons on defendant Nos. 2, 3 and 8.</u>

<u>22. I have very meticulously gone through the judgments of the Courts below, but I have not found from the findings of the Courts below that the Courts below have considered such vital aspects of the case, but passed the orders only on surmises.</u>

<u>23. In the view of the mater, the decisions referred to above by the learned Advocate for the petitioners to support his contention that the prima facie onus is on the plaintiffs to have served the summons or notices upon the defendants but we do not find as discussed above that summons were served upon the aforesaid defendant Nos. 2, 3, and 8. I do not also find any order of service of notice dated 10-8-1986 as referred by the learned Judge. Mr Alam for the plaintiff opposite parties has cited several cases of apex Court of the country to support his contentions but nobody can dispute the principle laid down by their Lordships in those cases, but we cannot use those decisions profitably in the facts and circumstances of the present case, in as such as we have already found that the summons were not served and that the Courts order also was not complied with by the plaintiffs and in this view of the Matter, we find substance in the submissions of the learned Advocate for the petitioners.</u>

<u>24. In view of my discussions made above, I find merit in the Rule. In the result, the rule is made absolute without any order as to costs and set aside the judgment and orders of the Courts below, The application under Order IX, rule 13 is allowed and the partition suit No. 1317 of 1985 is restored. The defendant petitioners are directed to pay legal expenses of Taka 10,000 to the plaintiff opposite parties within 2(two) months from the receipt of the notice from the Trial Court, failing which the order shall stand cancelled. The Trial Court is also directed to dispose Of the suit within 6 months from the date of receipt of the records.</u>
